inline.s: Last time someone asked: that sentient beings can perfect the wisdom of the Buddha, that much can be allowed; but how can the insentient do so? How can bricks and tiles, wood and stone perfect the wisdom of the Buddha? How can they become Buddhas? Today I shall speak of this again. Bricks and tiles, wood and stone are all our own intrinsic nature. Who is it that discovers bricks and tiles, wood and stone? Is it not our numinous light shining upon them that discovers them? And what is this numinous light? It is our Buddha-nature! Wherever the numinous light of our Buddha-nature shines, all sentient and insentient things, mountains and rivers, the great earth, sun, moon and stars, men and women, young and old, birds and beasts, are all shadows of Buddha-nature, all manifestations of Buddha-nature. You are a Buddha; then everything your numinous light shines upon is Buddha! Take a country: I am its king, and there is nothing in the land that is not mine. By the same token, you are a Buddha; the light of your Buddha-nature shines brilliantly through the ten directions, filling all space and the whole Dharma-realm, and there is nothing that is not illuminated by the numinous light of Buddha-nature. Therefore all things are Buddha, not one of them is not Buddha. But if our practice is not well done, if we do not know its lively and wondrous functioning and instead crush our thoughts to death, then we turn into earth, wood, metal and stone. Long ago two men practicing on a mountainside sat there without moving, and grass grew from their heads and out of their ears: they had turned into wood and stone. That was the result of the practice of crushing thought to death. So everything is ourselves, everything is our Buddha-nature, and every form we see is Buddha. For this reason stools, chairs, tables, desks and the rest are all Buddha, not one of them is not Buddha. Hence it is said: luxuriant yellow flowers are none other than prajñā; green green bamboo is all the dharmakāya. Flowers and bamboo alike are transformations of Buddha-nature; they are all Buddha! This question looks very hard to understand, but once the principle is clear it is not hard at all. Let me now tell a public case to discuss this question.

Long ago Chan Master Dongshan Liangjia could not understand this question either. He went to Patriarch Guishan to inquire, and asked: “I have heard that National Master Zhong of Nanyang had words on the insentient preaching the Dharma; I have not yet fathomed their subtlety.” Guishan asked: “Do you remember them?” Dongshan answered: “I remember.” Guishan said: “Try reciting them once for me.” So Dongshan recounted the matter.

A monk asked: ‘What is the mind of the ancient Buddhas?’ The National Master answered: ‘Walls and tiles are.’ The monk asked: ‘Are not walls and tiles insentient?’ (Walls and tiles are dull and dull-witted, without awareness, whereas the Buddha is the Awakened One, knowing all and capable of all. Walls and tiles have no awareness, are dull and dull-witted; how could they be the mind of the ancient Buddhas? By your account, walls and tiles would not be insentient either? This was the monk's rejoinder.) The National Master answered: ‘They are.’ (These words hold a profound meaning. Because sentient and insentient alike perfect the wisdom of the Buddha, it is only because of discrimination that the difference between sentient and insentient arises. If one does not discriminate, then all sounds and forms, mountains and rivers, the great earth, and even food and drink, men and women, are all perfected within the mind-nature, and not a single dharma is obtainable; what sentient or insentient could there then be? Because dharmas are held to be obtainable, one goes on to sort them into categories, to love and hate, to accept and reject, and so afflictions spring up in clusters and the wheel turns without cease. As said before, our body is originally a false union of the four great elements, just like the insentient. Only because the true mind is wrapped about by ignorance does it become the deluded mind, bound inside this shell of the four great elements and clung to as the self, and only thus does deluded knowing arise. Otherwise, would our bodies not be just the same as walls and tiles? But this monk did not understand this principle, and so had the following doubts.) The monk asked: ‘Does it also expound the Dharma?’ (Because the Buddha expounds the Dharma to save beings, and the ancient Buddhas did expound the Dharma; since the insentient is the mind of the ancient Buddhas, it must surely expound the Dharma too. This monk was like us ordinary beings, always falling into the sights and sounds of the dust-realms, never seeing the nature that can see and can hear.) The National Master answered: ‘It speaks constantly, it speaks blazingly. Without interruption.’ (The insentient preaching the Dharma is not intermittent, speaking at one time and not at another; it speaks at every hour and every moment, and the sound of its preaching is very loud, like a fiercely blazing great fire, and its preaching never pauses. We for our part always fix on what is seen and heard, not knowing that non-speaking is the true speaking. When a sound is heard, that is hearing; when no sound is heard, that is not hearing. In fact, not hearing a sound is also hearing! You hear a no-sound! Therefore non-speaking is true speaking: because the great sound is rare in its sound, the greatest sound is no sound. To say that there is a sound that can be heard is never true hearing, for you have fixed on what is heard. The nature of hearing does not lie in sound or in no-sound. Sound has arising and ceasing, and so is false; the nature has no place of cutting off, and so is true.) The monk asked: ‘Why do I not hear it?’ The National Master answered: ‘You yourself do not hear it; you cannot hinder another's hearing of it.’ (This is your own not hearing: because you are muddled about Buddha-nature and fix on there being a sound to be heard, you do not know that no-hearing is true hearing. Look further: who is it that hears the unheard? Who is it that hears no sound? You say you do not hear, yet it is shining at your ear-faculty — why do you not know it? You hear a no-sound; is that not hearing? To hear a no-sound, is that not true hearing? When you hear a sound, you follow the sound into discrimination and run off after it. But in this no-sound and no-discrimination, it is precisely when your hearing-nature is present before you; therefore it is true hearing. You yourself do not hear, but you cannot hinder that which can hear! Here the National Master rebuked, pointed out to, and reminded that monk. At this time when no sound is heard and the hearing-nature is truly hearing, you say you do not hear: it is you yourself who are not alert, not clear — yet the hearing-nature is still vividly and distinctly there!) The monk asked: ‘I wonder who can hear it.’ (In all the great earth there is not one person who does not hear. Who does not hear? Who lacks the hearing-nature? Only if one does not cling to sound, who then is not luminous with the hearing-nature? A pity that one's own eye-light does not so much as glance at it!) The National Master answered: ‘The sages hear it.’ (Buddhas, bodhisattvas, arhats, pratyekabuddhas and other sages can hear it; ordinary beings cannot. This answer of the National Master has a flaw, for everyone is originally a Buddha, the dharmakāya is without marks, ordinary and sage are not established — what sage or non-sage could there still be? Pressed hard by this, the National Master used these words to cover his eyes for the moment, yet the monk saw through him and questioned him further.) The monk asked: ‘Does the Master hear it or not?’ (Can you yourself hear it? Because the National Master had said the sages hear it, this question pressed him until he had no words. If he said he heard, that would be praising himself; if he said he did not hear, then the National Master would be no sage and no master.) The National Master answered: ‘I do not hear it.’ (He could only confess and plead guilty.) The monk asked: ‘Since the Master does not hear it, how do you know the insentient expounds the Dharma?’ (A good question, full of power: using the National Master's own spear to jab the National Master, leaving him nowhere to flee.) The National Master answered: ‘It is lucky that I do not hear it. If I heard it, I would be equal to the sages, and you would not hear me expound the Dharma.’ (Luckily I cannot hear it: if I heard it, I would be a sage, and you would not hear me expound the Dharma. This question was hard to evade, but the National Master was an adept in Chan and had his own place to turn. ‘It is lucky that I do not hear it’ — a clever flick, turning danger into safety. Yet whatever is spoken has no true meaning. Originally there is no dharma to speak and originally no one hears the Dharma. If there is still a dharma to speak and someone to hear it, that is precisely clinging to the mark of person and the mark of self. Hence when the National Master says, ‘You would not hear me expound the Dharma,’ he too is slandering himself.) The monk pressed him hard: ‘Then sentient beings have no part in it.’ (If so, sentient beings cannot hear the insentient preach the Dharma, and attainment of the Way is hopeless?) The National Master answered: ‘I speak for sentient beings, not for the sages.’ (The National Master turned the point of his words.) The monk asked: ‘After sentient beings hear it, what then?’ (This monk kept the National Master pinned fast: after sentient beings hear you speak, what happens?) The National Master answered: ‘Then they are not sentient beings.’ (The National Master pushed the boat with the current and turned the monk's sharp point aside. If sentient beings can hear the insentient preach the Dharma and take up this unborn, undying hearing-nature, then they transcend the ordinary and enter the sage, and so he says, ‘then they are not sentient beings.’ The Diamond Sutra says: ‘Sentient beings, sentient beings — the Tathāgata says they are not sentient beings, therefore they are called sentient beings.’ Sentient beings? Where are there sentient beings? All sentient beings are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, none of them real. The reason sentient beings are sentient beings is simply that they do not awaken; if they awaken in this very moment, they are not sentient beings. Yet while in the dream they do not awaken, they cannot but be sentient beings, and so it is said they are called sentient beings. Therefore awaken quickly from the dream! Someone once said: you say everything is nothing? Suppose my ear is struck deaf and cannot hear sounds — still, this is there! That my ear is deaf is still a phenomenon, it cannot be emptied. This is clinging to marks with a sticky mind, not awakening! Wake up quickly! Do not dream on. For example, in a dream we are beaten, or our head is cut off, but on waking we have not been beaten nor killed, and our head is quite well. Your ear struck deaf: in fact this deafness is an illusory false appearance, just like being beaten and killed in a dream, unobtainable. So do not cling to the dream; empty it quickly! Awaken quickly! After waking, nothing is left! When Lord Guan had his head cut off by Lü Meng, he cried out in agony: ‘Give me back my head, give me back my head!’ When he learned of it, Great Master Zhiyi went to save him. The Master sat cross-legged and blocked Lord Guan's path. Lord Guan thought: this monk is very bold, daring to block my way — I shall teach him a lesson. Thereupon, whuo — a wild wind arose, flying sand and stones struck at his face, but Great Master Zhiyi did not move a hair. Lord Guan thought: you do not fear wild wind and flying sand; then I shall bring a great mountain to frighten you. Thereupon a great mountain came pressing down, covering sky and earth, and still Great Master Zhiyi did not move a hair. Now Lord Guan was filled with admiration: this monk has true skill! He quickly stepped forward and bowed. Then Great Master Zhiyi expounded the Dharma for Lord Guan: ‘Here you cry, Give me back my head, give me back my head. Someone cut off one of your heads and you demand it back — how many heads did you cut off in your life? Can you give them back? Besides, though your head is gone, you lack nothing at all! Why? Because you have only lost this illusory form-body; your numinous knowing, your true mind, lacks not the least bit.’ We have said that one should take emptiness-and-stillness as the substance and not acknowledge the form-body as the substance; space alone is my true body, the husk is not the true body but only a house. Take the numinous knowing as mind, and do not acknowledge delusive thoughts and delusive notions as mind; delusive notions and delusive thoughts are not real but are things that cling to marks and climb after objects. The nature of numinous knowing is the knowing-nature that knows cold and heat, knows pain and itch; it does not abide in marks, and this thing has no head and no tail, no name and no word. Long ago the Sixth Patriarch, Great Master Huineng, asked the assembly: ‘I have one thing: no head, no tail, no name, no word, no back, no front. Do you all know it?’ Shenhui came forward and said: ‘It is the source of all Buddhas, Shenhui's Buddha-nature.’ The Sixth Patriarch said: ‘I told you it has no name and no word, and you call it the source, Buddha-nature. Later on you will set up a hut over your head and be no more than a doctrinal adherent of intellectual understanding.’ The nature of numinous knowing — its intrinsic nature is without marks and without name; to say it resembles a thing misses it at once. Shenhui added a name to it, and that was already delusive thought. Therefore we should not acknowledge delusive thought as mind, but should acknowledge the nature of numinous knowing. This is the Dharma that Great Master Zhiyi expounded for Lord Guan: that you feel your head ache is the deluded-thought mind's clinging; your husk is already ruined, already gone — what pain is left? Once the mind is empty, you shine with great light, Buddha-nature is luminous, and what pain or no-pain is there! After Lord Guan was thus pointed out to by Zhiyi, he awakened, and thereupon vowed to become a Dharma-protecting spirit. So sentient beings need only wake from the dream and take up the unborn, undying intrinsic nature, and then they transcend the ordinary and enter the sage and are not sentient beings. Therefore, when National Master Zhong of Nanyang said that after sentient beings hear the insentient preach the Dharma they are not sentient beings, that is what he meant.) The monk asked again: ‘The insentient preaching the Dharma — on what scripture is it based?’ (That the insentient can preach the Dharma — I have never heard of it; is there a basis? From what scripture does it come? Surely you did not invent it yourself? This monk stuck fast to the National Master and would not let go.) The National Master answered: ‘Indeed. If one's words do not accord with the scriptures, they are not what a gentleman speaks of. Have you not seen what the Avataṃsaka Sutra says: lands speak, sentient beings speak, all three times speak.’ (The National Master is saying that of course you are quite right: if the insentient preaching the Dharma had no basis, no scriptural authority, it would have no meaning at all and would not be a gentleman's words either. Then he brought out scripture: the Avataṃsaka Sutra says, lands speak, sentient beings speak, all three times speak. That is, every mote of dust, every land is speaking the Dharma; every sentient being contains all; whether the sentient world or the insentient world, there is nowhere that is not speaking the Dharma; past, present and future — the dharmas of the three times are nowhere not speaking the Dharma!)” This was National Master Zhong of Nanyang's instruction to that monk. Chan Master Dongshan did not understand it, and so he recounted this public case to Patriarch Guishan.

After hearing it, Guishan said: “I too have this here; only I seldom meet the right person.” This insentient preaching of the Dharma — I too have it here. Only when one meets a person of comparable capacity can the opportunity meet the opportunity, and so he says, “seldom meet the right person.” Dongshan Liangjia earnestly requested: “I am not clear; I beg the Master to instruct me.” Guishan raised his fly-whisk and said: “Do you understand?” This is the insentient preaching the Dharma — can you comprehend it? The insentient preaching the Dharma has no sound, yet it is not that it does not speak. When flowers bloom and fall, that too is the insentient speaking the Dharma. Flowers are insentient; a flower opens, tender and beautiful, but before long it withers and scatters — what Dharma is this speaking? It speaks the Dharma of impermanence. The river flows on with a hua, hua — the flowing water does not abide, it does not stay; it flows past today like this and tomorrow like this, never resting. This flowing water tells us: the false marks of the ten thousand things change, but the true substance never alters. Su Dongpo understood this principle and said: “What passes is like this, and yet it never goes.” Flowing water is insentient, yet it too speaks the Dharma. So the insentient is speaking the Dharma at every moment; it is not that it does not speak, only that you yourself do not know it. Thus Guishan's raising of the fly-whisk means to ask: who is it that raises the fly-whisk? It is not only by opening the mouth that one speaks the Dharma; this one raising is itself speaking the Dharma.

But Dongshan Liangjia still did not understand and did not comprehend, so he said: “I do not understand.” Dongshan honestly admitted that he did not understand and had not grasped it. In truth, at such a moment one is closest to it. For if you understand and comprehend it, that is emotional view and there is a principle to be had. On the contrary, when you do not understand, that is precisely the time when not one thought arises; turn the light around at once — what is this? In that instant you see the nature. A pity that Dongshan always supposed there was still a principle to be had, mistook the meaning, and let the opportunity slip. Dongshan went on: “I beg the Master to speak.” Guishan said: “A mouth born of parents will never speak it for you.” This flesh mouth born of father and mother can never tell it to you. Why? Because no matter how much you say, it is never said. This is what words cannot reach and thought cannot arrive at: “the path of language is cut off, the place of mental activity is extinguished.” Say it and you miss it; know it and it is not it. Here Guishan was hinting to Dongshan that non-speaking is true speaking and non-hearing is true hearing; this is the insentient preaching the Dharma. Sadly, at this moment Dongshan was still muddled and did not understand. People always cling to the six dust-objects — form, sound, smell, taste, touch, dharmas — which the seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing confront, that is, they cling to what is seen and heard; and then what is unseen and unheard is not it. They do not know that this true nature which can see and can hear in the absence of the seen and heard is never interrupted, leaves no trace of continuity, and is thus, thus unmoving. Hence Buddha-nature is also called “thusness.” From this we can see how thick and heavy people's habit of delusive thought and clinging is!

Moreover, Chan Master Guishan's “A mouth born of parents will never speak it for you” has another layer of meaning: the work must be done by oneself alone, and Buddha-nature must be awakened to by oneself. The ancients said: “What enters by the door is not the family treasure.” What you hear in through the ear enters by the door, for the gates of the six faculties all face outward. The principle heard in through the ear is not your own treasure. Only what you awaken to yourself is true. For me to explain it to you does you not the least good, and in the future you will resent me for it.

Speaking of this, I am reminded of Patriarch Xiangyan, who met this same question. Patriarch Xiangyan and Patriarch Guishan were both disciples of Patriarch Baizhang. Xiangyan was thoroughly familiar with the Buddhist scriptures; if someone asked him about the Dharma, he would often answer ten times over for one question, and he thought himself quite extraordinary, privately reckoning: my wisdom is like the sea! Yet while Baizhang was alive he did not attain in Chan. After Baizhang passed into nirvāṇa, he had no choice but to go to his senior brother Guishan to practice Chan. Guishan said to him: “Junior brother! I hear that with our late master Baizhang you answered ten for one question and a hundred for ten.” He quickly said: “Not at all, not at all.” Guishan said: “That is your cleverness and sharpness, your conceptual understanding and intellectual reckoning — the root of birth and death. Now I have a question to ask you; give me an answer and let me see.” On the surface he asked lightly: “What question is it?” But in his heart he was saying: “What question could there be that I cannot answer? Hmph!” Guishan said: “I will not ask you about anything else, only this: before your parents gave birth to you, what was your original face? Try and say one phrase.” When Xiangyan heard this, his mind went utterly blank. So he returned to his quarters and read through all the scriptures and commentaries he had studied, from beginning to end, seeking one phrase with which to answer — and in the end he got nothing at all. He sighed: “A painted cake cannot fill hunger.” Then he begged Guishan again and again to explain it. Guishan said: “If I explained it to you, you would curse me later on. What I say is mine and in the end has nothing to do with you. You had better go and look into it yourself!” Thereupon Xiangyan burned all the writings he had studied, took leave of Guishan, and went off to look into it on his own. He looked into it morning and evening, looked into it at all times, walking, standing, sitting and lying down. One day he was weeding in the field; as his hoe came down it struck a stone. He picked the stone up and tossed it away at random; it hit a bamboo — “crack!” — and he suddenly awakened and saw his original face. Then he went back, bathed and burned incense, and bowed from afar to his senior brother Guishan, praising him: “Great is the Master's compassion, a kindness surpassing that of my parents. Had you explained it to me then, how would today's matter have come about?”

So the work must be done by oneself. Therefore Patriarch Guishan said to Dongshan: “A mouth born of parents will never speak it for you. If I told you, it would be of no use; you must look into it yourself!” Chan Master Dongshan Liangjia could not awaken, and feeling that the opportunity did not match, he asked again: “Is there anyone else who seeks the Way at the same time as the Master?” Thereupon Guishan directed him to go and study under Chan Master Yunyao.

We have said before that a person has two bad things: one is emotion, the other is thought. If deluded emotion and love were cut off, all would be well. Why? Because emotion is born of love, and love can produce water; the nature of water is to flow downward and it cannot rise to heaven, and so it must be cut off. For example, when we meet something we love to eat, saliva comes; if someone dear to us is about to leave, or to set out on a long journey, tears flow out unbidden; and if a dear one dies, we weep all the more bitterly; as for men and women in love, there is no need even to speak of it. The nature of water is moisture, and whatever water it is, it is moist and it flows downward. So the “emotion” in love-emotion sinks downward; but if we wish to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, we must rise and fly — sinking down leaves no hope. Therefore emotional views must be cut off completely. If love-emotion is not cut off completely, one cannot be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and so emotion is a bad thing. Thought is somewhat better, but this thought is not random thinking — random thinking is still emotion. Only because we have emotion do we think randomly. For example, if we love someone, we think up every way to get that person into our hands; if that person has a partner, we think up some way to get rid of the partner and then get the person. You see, plays and novels are all written like that — without it there would be no plays or novels. This is creating karma! Creating karma means undergoing its retribution. Random thinking is in fact love-emotion, and it still will not do.

Then what is this thought? It is secretly thinking about the method of practice: thinking how we may escape this realm of the sentient, and realize our original face; or thinking of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, tying the mind to the West and reciting the Buddha-name with effort — that is better. But speaking from the ultimate point, thought and emotion are equally unworkable. Why? Without emotion how could there be thought, and without thought how could there be emotion? Emotion and thought are not separate. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says that if we truly cultivate contemplative visualization in secret, and the seventh consciousness can leave our bodily form, or transform into whatever is visualized, this is called “pure thought, therefore flying” — but it is not yet truly pure. When truly pure, even thought is gone. If there is still a Buddha to be mindful of, that is not yet truly pure; when truly pure there is nothing at all, and that alone is the Pure Land of Eternal Stillness and Light. But in reciting the Buddha-name and seeking birth in the West we need not set our demands too high: to be born in the Land of Coexistence of Sages and Ordinary Beings is quite enough. So when Buddha-recitation reaches the point where emotion is cut off, pure thought flies, and one can be reborn in the West — it is no hard matter! In practice one should think only of how good it is to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, of how Amitābha Buddha's light shines, of how he receives and welcomes us; and when the time of passing comes and we fly upward, the holy realm of the West will appear of itself, and we shall see Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva and all the bodhisattvas come to welcome us, and we shall fly to birth in the West. “Pure thought, therefore flying” is the wholesome root of one's pure Buddha-recitation karma ripening and manifesting the holy realm. We now speak of the Pure Land as only one West, but the Śūraṅgama Sutra speaks of the pure lands of the ten directions, and one is reborn there according to one's conditions — not only in the Western Pure Land. From this we know that if one wishes to be born in a pure land, one must cut off this love-emotion and deluded emotion entirely.

Therefore all cultivators who have attained are without emotional views; if you have emotion, it will not do. What is a bodhisattva? It is the abbreviation of the Sanskrit “bodhisattva,” rendered into Chinese as “awakening being” — that is, one first awakens through and breaks all one's own emotional views, does not cling to any sound, form, dust or object, and clearly awakens to the intrinsic nature; only then can one help others break through the deluded dream, sweep away deluded emotion, and escape the sea of suffering together. Hence Chan Master Yunyao said, “The insentient hear it.”

Dongshan pressed him closely: “Does the Master hear it?” To this point Dongshan was still a muddled fellow. Yunyao answered: “If I heard it, you would not hear me expound the Dharma.” This is exactly the same as National Master Zhong. If I could hear it, I would not expound the Dharma for you. Why? First, if I heard it, I would be equal to the sages; and the reward-body and transformation-body of the sages are not true, nor are they speakers of the Dharma — the true dharmakāya of the sages neither speaks nor hears. If I heard it, I would have attained the Way just like the Buddhas and bodhisattvas; neither ordinary nor sage would be obtainable, neither ordinary nor sage would be abided in, and all would be nothing — could you then still hear me expound the Dharma? Note this! “All would be nothing” is not a nihilistic void. It is to have and yet not abide, to speak and yet not speak, not to speak and yet to speak; not to stubbornly insist on not speaking, and still less to cling to there being something spoken. All activities are empty contrivances; there is no Buddha either — even the word “Buddha” is a provisional false name! If there were still something for the Buddhas to go beyond, the Buddha would not be Buddha! So we should not abide in marks; true attainment of the Way is not a single thing. Second, if I heard it, I would be the same as the insentient; and the insentient takes not speaking as true speaking, having no words — so how could you today hear me expound the Dharma? Third, if I heard it, I would cling to the dust of sound, have something to abide in, and my Dharma-view would not be removed — how could I be anyone's teacher? Therefore I do not hear it. No-hearing is true hearing! That is, “no words” — there are no words to speak. You must earnestly grasp the meaning beyond the words! You understand only the Dharma that has language, the Dharma that can be spoken; and these words you now hear me speaking all have words, and none of them is real. But in speaking to you thus, I want you to grasp the meaning beyond the words, to understand the meaning outside the words, and thereby clearly see the true speaking that is no-speaking and the true hearing that is no-hearing. Yet Dongshan still did not grasp it, and asked again: “Why do I not hear it?” He asked Yunyao: “The insentient preaching the Dharma — I ought to hear it; why do I not hear it?” He was still clinging to the dust-realms of sound and form. What meaning is there in chasing after that? Why not turn the hearing around and hear the self-nature? It is shining at your face right now! Is this not your hearing naturally, your hearing in no-hearing? People in the world are all so muddled — how pitiable! At this moment Yunyao, like Guishan, raised his fly-whisk. If Dongshan had seized this moment and asked himself, “Who is it that sees the fly-whisk raised?” and brought forth his spirit right there, he would have awakened on the spot. A pity, a pity — he missed it again! Yunyao asked: “Do you hear it?” Though the raised fly-whisk makes no sound and has no words, yet the great sound is rare in its sound, utterly real and distinct, like thunder splitting the ear. Why? Because the sound of no-sound is the greatest sound; this is what is meant by “the great sound is rare in its sound.”

We people always cling to there being a sound to hear, and we try to understand at the place where sound can be heard. But if you would truly see the nature, you must not cling to the place where sound can be heard. For sound and no-sound are merely the arising and ceasing of sound, whereas our hearing-nature is shining before us at every moment; it has no interval and no continuity. Hence the ancients said: “Peach blossoms on both banks after wind and rain — where can a horse's hooves avoid the fallen red?” On both sides of a narrow path peach trees were planted all along; after a great wind and rain the path was covered everywhere with peach petals — riding through, how could the horse's hooves avoid the petals all over the ground and not tread on them? The meaning is that Buddha-nature functions at all times and in all places; it is nowhere absent and never not present — can you avoid it? So do not discriminate between having marks and having no marks, between sound and no sound. When we cannot see light, we do see darkness, and seeing darkness is still seeing. When we cannot hear sound, we hear no-sound, and hearing no-sound is still hearing. Is this not proof that the seeing-nature and the hearing-nature neither arise nor cease?

A pity that Dongshan answered: “I do not hear it.” He was clinging to sound: because he heard no sound, he did not hear. This is like casting a coy glance at a blind man — he missed it right before his face, what a pity! Yet we must say: it is fortunate that he did not hear; had he heard, he would again have clung to marks — whereas no-hearing is true hearing. Yunyao said: “When I expound the Dharma you still do not hear it — how much less the insentient preaching the Dharma?” Thus do I expound the Dharma for you: I raised the fly-whisk — though there was no sound, there was still a movement — and even this you did not hear and did not understand; how much less the true speaking and true moving that neither speaks nor moves! People in the world are all so foolish: they cling to the deluded karma of form and sound in what they see and hear, and never once turn the light around for a glance to take up this nature that can see and hear, can speak and move. This nature is the original true Buddha! Some even mistakenly think that to hear no sound is to have no hearing, and to see no light, shadow, form or mark is to have no seeing. They do not know that this seeing-nature and hearing-nature are shining at the face at every moment, never covered and never interrupted. Even when there is no sound to hear and no mark to see, there is still seeing and still hearing. For when you hear a no-sound, that is still hearing, and when you see a no-mark, that is still seeing — how can you say there is no seeing and no hearing?

Dongshan then asked again: “The insentient preaching the Dharma — on which scripture is it based?” just as the monk in the earlier public case asked the National Master. Chan Master Yunyao answered: “Have you not seen what the Amitābha Sutra says: the water, the birds and the trees all recite the Buddha and recite the Dharma.” At this Chan Master Dongshan Liangjia suddenly had something of an awakening: he had at last entered no-sound by way of sound, and had at any rate grasped it and awakened to it. He blurted out a verse: “How wondrous, how wondrous! / The insentient preaching the Dharma is inconceivable. / If you listen with the ear, you will never grasp it; / Hearing the sound at the eye — only then do you know.” Truly wondrous, truly strange! That the insentient can preach the Dharma is so wondrous it cannot be put into words, so inconceivable that no one could imagine it! Can the insentient preach the Dharma? Yes! If you listen with the ear, you cannot understand it, because the insentient preaching the Dharma has no sound. Only by hearing with the eye can you grasp the wonder of it. The eye does not hear sound, yet this very no-sound is the wondrous sound. From this we see that Chan Master Dongshan grasped sound, and moreover went from sound to no-sound; but he had not yet grasped that no-sound is sound and sound is no-sound — he had not yet reached the ultimate.

There are many more public cases of awakening to the Way through sound. Let me give one more example. Long ago Chan Master Yuanwu Qin was a personal attendant under Chan Master Wuzu Yan, practicing Chan along with Master Yan. One day a scholar came to consult Wuzu Yan, and Wuzu Yan said to him: “If you ask about self-nature and the dharmakāya, did you read the ‘little love poem’ in your youth? Two lines in it are very close to it: ‘Calling Little Jade so often was nothing at all; / She only wanted her gallant to know her voice.’” The meaning is that she calls again and again, “Little Jade! Little Jade!” Little Jade is a maidservant — what business did the young lady have with her? None. Then why call? The purpose was to let her sweetheart hear the call and know she was there. That is, she deliberately sent her sweetheart a message, because he knew her voice, and hearing the call would know she was there. This borrows a poem to speak of Chan. Borrowing the poem to ask back: who is it that utters this call, and who is it that hears it? Are not all these the functioning of the self-nature? Are they not all the manifestation of the true nature? Chan Master Wuzu Yan's quotation of this little love poem contains a deep meaning. Originally all forms and all sounds are meaningless, all are flowers in the sky and moons in the water, all unobtainable — which matches the first line, “nothing at all.” But all things are the functioning of the self-nature, all are the manifestation of the true nature — which matches the second line, “know her voice.” This is meant to awaken us all to recognize our own original face. Yuanwu Qin heard these words from the side and was at once somewhat awakened. He walked out of the abbot's quarters, and just then a big rooster crowed long on the fence, “awk, awk.” The moment Yuanwu Qin heard it, his spiritual opportunity was suddenly stirred; he was struck by the word “voice” in what Wuzu Yan had just said, “She only wanted her gallant to know her voice,” and he suddenly awakened greatly! Is this not voice? This is the manifestation of the self-nature; all shadows cannot leave the mirror — apart from the mirror, where would the shadows be? Every last thing is the functioning of the true nature, is the manifestation of the true nature.

From the explanations of these several public cases above, we should not misinterpret “hearing the sound at the eye” as some special psychic power. Quite a few cultivators are fond of superknowledges, and often mistakenly suppose that only when the ear can read words and the eye can hear sounds, when the six faculties are used interchangeably and superknowledges are produced, can one hear the insentient preaching the Dharma. They do not know that the insentient preaching the Dharma is speaking without speaking; it is not that there is a subtle sound which you can hear only when you stop listening with the ear and looking with the eye. “Hearing the sound at the eye” is not a special power. Chan Master Dongshan's “Hearing the sound at the eye — only then do you know” tells us not to abide on the ear-faculty, but, where there is no sound to hear, where delusive thoughts do not arise, where a scene stirs feeling, to turn the light around and inwardly comprehend this wondrous numinous true mind that is unborn in a single thought and yet vividly distinct. When you recognize your own original face and understand that every last thing is the functioning of the true mind and the manifestation of the true mind, then you can understand that “the insentient is the sentient, and the sentient is the insentient.” Mountains and rivers, the great earth, sun, moon and stars, walls and tiles and the rest — they are ourselves! Why? Are not mountains and rivers, the great earth and the rest within space? Can they go outside space? No. Our true mind is like space: as vast as space is, so vast is our true mind. The true mind pervades space and exhausts the Dharma-realm; the ten Dharma-realms are all within my mind, and everything in space is within my mind — so mountains and rivers, the great earth and the rest do not go outside my mind either. The Zuo Commentary says: “Under the whole heaven there is no land that is not the king's; to the shores of every stream there is no one who is not the king's servant.” I am a Buddha, and they are Buddhas too — all are Buddha! Hence “the insentient is the sentient, and the sentient is the insentient”! Again, the insentient is earth, water, fire and wind! The earth, for instance, is composed of the four great elements, earth, water, fire and wind: the earth turns, rotating on its axis and revolving in orbit, and motion is wind; the earth has a crust, and the crust is hard — that is the great element earth; on the earth's surface and beneath it there is water — that is the great element water; the earth's core is red-hot molten matter, and volcanoes often erupt on the surface — that is the great element fire. Earth, water, fire and wind are all present: the earth is compounded of the four great seed-natures, earth, water, fire and wind. A seed-nature is so called because a seed can bring things forth; thus the four great seed-natures can bring forth the ten thousand things. Our Buddha-nature has seven great components — earth, water, fire, wind, space, faculty and consciousness — and so is called the seven great seed-natures. Everything in the world is brought forth by these seven great seed-natures: “sentient and insentient alike perfect the wisdom of the Buddha.” Therefore the insentient is the sentient and the sentient is the insentient; whether sentient or insentient, all is ourselves. Since all is ourselves, what sentient-and-insentient distinction can there be? Understanding this principle, you know that the table too is Buddha, the chair too is Buddha, a brick too is Buddha, a tile too is Buddha — not one is not Buddha. All sentient and insentient things are Buddha!

First point: all insentient things are things of the wondrous luminous true mind, and the true mind is the Buddha-mind; therefore the insentient is the sentient. The true mind is not as our deluded minds imagine — covered by ignorance and shrunk to the size of a little dot inside the husk. When you have done the work and broken it open, you find that it is all space and the whole Dharma-realm: as vast as space is, so vast is the true mind. Chan Master Xuefeng Yicun said: “The true mind is like an ancient mirror: however broad and great space is, the ancient mirror is that broad and great.” Why say it is like an ancient mirror? An ancient mirror means one that does not exist only in this age; it is compared to our true mind, which has existed since beginningless time. And why compare it to a mirror? Because a mirror can reflect the ten thousand things, and the myriad phenomena can appear in the mirror; our true mind is like this too — it brightly illumines the great chiliocosm, and its measure encompasses the sand-grain worlds without obstruction. Sand-grain worlds are the immeasurable, boundless worlds, as many as the sands of the Ganges and beyond counting. There are very many worlds in space; science now proves that there are beings on other planets, and stars like the sun are more than one. The more science advances, the more it proves that what our Buddha said is true and not false. Our true mind is like space: all worlds are within our mind; and if the worlds are within our mind, is the insentient not within our mind? The houses we build are insentient, and they are on the earth, and the earth is in space — so are the houses not in space too? Therefore all insentient things are within my mind! Because they are within our mind, we say that our true mind is spiritually complete with the ten thousand things. The ten thousand things are within our true mind, and the true mind is the Buddha-mind — what are the ten thousand things if not Buddha? Hence it is said that there is no distinction between sentient and insentient. Why must this principle be made clear? Because when you understand that the insentient is the sentient, your mind becomes vast and can contain the ten thousand things, and you no longer cling to marks and grasp and seize; only then does practice advance easily. Therefore we must have a correct and clear understanding that the insentient is the sentient. This is the first point.

Second point: all insentient things are nothing but the four great elements, and the four great elements are the elemental seeds of the true mind. The earth, for example, is insentient, and it too is composed of the four great elements, earth, water, fire and wind; so is a great tree, composed of the four great elements and likewise insentient — none of them has love or emotion. The earth's motion, its rotation and revolution — is that not the great element wind? The crust is hard — is that not the great element earth? On the surface there are oceans, and underground there is groundwater — is that not the great element water? In the earth's core there is fire, and when a volcano erupts the fire comes out — is that not the great element fire? So all is earth, water, fire and wind. The same with a tree: it sways without cease — is that not the great element wind? The trunk is the great element earth; strip off the bark and water comes out — that is the great element water; the tree itself has the nature of fire and can burn — is that not the great element fire? So all is made of the four great elements. And the four great elements, earth, water, fire and wind, are the basic elements of our Buddha-nature; they are the four great seed-natures. A seed-nature is a seed that can bring things forth — like rice seed and wheat seed: plant rice seed and rice grows, plant wheat seed and wheat grows. So a seed means the capacity to produce and to grow. Therefore our Buddha-nature is an all-capable substance: all things are created by it, all things are invented by it, all things are manifested by it — so all things are our Buddha-nature! Do not suppose they are things outside the body; they are all ourselves!

Third point: who is it that discovers the insentient, and who is it that makes it? Apart from our Buddha-nature it cannot be discovered. Suppose there is a tree here with a flower on it; if we do not look at it, who can know there is a flower on the tree? Then who is it that sees the flower? Is it the eye? It is not the eye. Modern scientists also understand that seeing things is not the work of the eye but of the brain, because if the brain does not function, the eye cannot function and nothing can be seen. But scientists only know that the brain can make the six faculties function; they cannot go further and know that the brain itself cannot function either. For the nerves of the brain are only like a power grid: to function they still need energy (electricity) fed in; if no energy (electricity) is fed in, the brain has no motive force and cannot function — just as an electric lamp cannot shine if the current does not come. And what is this energy? It is our Buddha-nature. When Buddha-nature departs, though the brain remains it cannot function. Therefore our every word and every deed, our every movement, is the wondrous functioning of Buddha-nature; apart from Buddha-nature we could not function at all. Hence that our eyes can see the insentient is the manifestation of Buddha-nature, and the insentient is likewise accomplished by Buddha-nature. Why? Suppose we have a thought: how shall this flower be planted, how shall it be nurtured? Then we study the art of growing flowers, tend them carefully, and the flowers bloom luxuriantly — what is this if not the working of our Buddha-nature? If a person's Buddha-nature left him, his body would be like a stone; could he still use his mind? Could his hands and feet still move? Could he still cultivate flowers? Who built the houses? People built them. If engineers, craftsmen and masons were apart from Buddha-nature, could their brains still work, could their hands and feet still move to design blueprints and build houses? So all insentient things are manifested by our Buddha-nature and accomplished by Buddha-nature. For this reason, apart from Buddha-nature there is no insentient thing at all. If the insentient departed from Buddha-nature, could it still be? Absolutely not. Therefore the insentient is the sentient, and is Buddha-nature. These insentient things are like the shadows shown in a mirror, and the mirror is like our true mind, our Buddha-nature. Our true mind, our Buddha-nature, is the great perfect mirror wisdom; it brightly illumines the ten directions without obstruction, and there is nothing in the worlds of the ten directions that it does not manifest and does not see. That a mirror reflects objects is only an analogy — it is not enough to describe the great perfect mirror wisdom. To see these things before you, or the light that issues before your eyes — is that the great perfect mirror wisdom? No, no, it is far from it! A mirror can show shadows, and the mind-mirror can illumine the ten thousand marks; shadows cannot leave the mirror. Can a shadow leave the mirror? Apart from the mirror the shadow is gone. The shadow cannot leave the mirror; marks cannot leave the mind. Apart from the mind, marks have nowhere to appear; and without shadows there is no mirror — likewise, apart from marks the true mind cannot be manifested. The true mind has no mark to be seen and must be manifested through things and marks. Therefore the true mind can accomplish the ten thousand things, and conversely the ten thousand things manifest the true mind — mind and mark are just this subtle. For this reason mind is mark and mark is mind, the shadow is the mirror and the mirror is the shadow; therefore the insentient is the sentient. This is the third point.

Fourth point: the insentient is originally Buddha-nature; only because of ignorance and non-awakening do we falsely take a small portion of the four great elements as our body, discard the greater part of the four great elements as things outside the body and judge them insentient — and so there is the delusive discrimination between sentient and insentient. From the examples analyzed above, all insentient things are originally manifested by Buddha-nature; it is only because of ignorance that sentient beings, without knowing or perceiving it, take a small portion of the four great elements (earth, water, fire, wind) as their own form-body, and discard more than ninety percent of the four great elements outside, regarding them as things outside the body; and then they discriminate: this is sentient, that is insentient. In fact all is oneself — this is the fault of ignorance! So if our practice has power and we break ignorance open, we can realize that these mountains and rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees and thickets are not one of them anything but ourselves. With me as the master, you and everything around are shadows in my mind; with you as the master, all this is a shadow in your mind. There is a good saying: every sentient being is complete with the whole Dharma-realm. What is the whole Dharma-realm? The Dharma-realm is the one true Dharma-realm, which is the true mind. That everything is complete and lacks not a hairsbreadth is called “the whole.” Whole in what? Whole in that each sentient being is complete with it; sentient beings may each be complete with it. You are you, I am I, he is he; Zhang San is Zhang San and Li Si is Li Si — each complete with what? Each is complete with the whole Dharma-realm: that is, every person has the true mind and lacks not a fraction. For example, your mirror contains me and my mirror contains you, mutually containing without hindrance; again, as with many electric lamps in a room, the light of this lamp and the light of that lamp blend light with light and contain light with light, mutually not excluding each other. From this we know that insentient and sentient are one body; only because of our ignorance and non-awakening do we falsely give rise to discrimination. When ignorance is broken, one can truly realize the wondrous functioning of the true mind, and will no longer regard the insentient as an external thing.

Fifth point: the insentient is earth, wood, metal and stone. If we do our work badly and crush delusive thought to death, then we turn insentient and become earth, wood, metal and stone; and earth, wood, metal and stone are one of our twelve classes of beings (the Diamond Sutra speaks of ten classes of beings, the Śūraṅgama Sutra of twelve). Some say the six realms of rebirth are all sentient and have nothing to do with the insentient. In fact, if you do your work badly, or practice an outside-path method and crush your thoughts to death, you too will transform into earth, wood, metal and stone and become insentient. So from this, is the sentient not the insentient?

So when you understand that mountains and rivers, the great earth, men and women, young and old, sentient and insentient are all manifestations of our Buddha-nature and are all ourselves, then in practice you should be empty and numinous, without abiding, neither seizing nor releasing. Not seizing means that when a delusive thought comes you do not press it down and forbid it to move, turning into earth, wood, metal and stone; not releasing means that you do not let delusive thoughts run wild and so wander through birth and death. Toward delusive thoughts neither press nor follow: let them come, pay them no heed. Delusive thoughts are not absent — they are present. Delusive thoughts formed over many lives and many kalpas: do you think that as soon as you begin to practice they will be gone? That is easier said than done; it cannot be done. So in our practice we first cut off coarse delusion. Coarse delusion is the delusive thinking produced when the mind reacts to objects. How do we put coarse delusion to rest? We must know that objects are unobtainable, that they are all shadows manifested by the self-nature; my true mind is the mirror and all those others are shadows — grasp the mirror, not the shadows. If you do not cling to shadow-marks, the true mind does not move and delusive thoughts do not arise; coarse delusion is put to rest. If coarse delusion is not put to rest, your sitting in meditation is sitting for nothing. For example, if while sitting you think of how your son is doing, how your daughter is, you cannot sit well. And if you go on in flights of fancy about how to spend your money, what to buy, how cheap things are there, how so-and-so is good and so-and-so is bad, and so on, can you still sit well? You cannot.

Coarse delusion must be put to rest; pay no attention to the shadows in the mind, for the shadows in a mirror cannot be grasped. Someone may say: the shadows in the mirror cannot be grasped, but the things that appear I can grasp — look, I have this pen in hand. Ah! You are dreaming; that is a dream-scene! In a dream the things do indeed seem graspable: you taste the good food and eat it, you talk happily with a good friend, you are terrified at meeting an enemy — but when the dream ends there is nothing at all. We are in a dream-scene right now; do not cling to marks, for nothing at all can be grasped. When the last breath does not come, you can take nothing with you; rather than having to let go in the future, why not let go early and save yourself some effort? If you want to wake up (to awaken), you must do the work. Those who recite the Buddha-name and those who hold mantras must concentrate the mind single-mindedly, cut off delusive thoughts, and let body, mind and world all vanish and empty out, until only the vivid true mind stands before them; then it is like waking from a dream — everything seen and gained in the dream is empty, gone — what is there left to grasp? So all present marks are shadows and cannot be sought after! Therefore it is now necessary to speak clearly to you, so that you understand the principle that the sentient is the insentient: do not go on in delusive discrimination — let go, let go. The insentient is the sentient and the sentient is the insentient; what mark are you still clinging to?

If you truly set your heart on it and put your whole being into it, then when you take your seat in practice you will enter samādhi easily. When coarse delusion is cut off, subtle delusion will still come to intrude; do not fear it and do not press it down, only pay it no heed, and where delusive thought is cut off the true mind appears. “When arising and ceasing cease, the still extinction appears before you” — this is nirvāṇa. The unborn and undying is nirvāṇa; arising and ceasing is the deluded mind. When delusive thoughts and delusive emotions are all extinguished, this unborn, undying Buddha-nature appears. Why is it that we cannot sit well in practice? We must examine ourselves: what is our mind still stuck to, and why are we still stuck to it? Let go of it at once! All things are shadows in our mind — why are you still stuck to them? They are unobtainable, false, empty — let go! When you truly let go, then whether you recite the Buddha-name or hold mantras, subject and object both vanish and faculties and dusts drop away, and Buddha-nature naturally appears and you awaken. Whether or not you have seen the nature, do not ask others — taste it for yourself. The supreme flavor of awakening is like a mute person's dream: it cannot be told to anyone, yet in the heart it is clear.

I have spoken again and again of the question of marks and no-marks, striving to speak it clearly and thoroughly, with the aim of setting everyone's view straight — which is also the essential meaning of the Mahāmudrā's first establishing of the view as the school. To take knowing and seeing as the school is the very heart of the Buddhadharma. When knowing and seeing are right and you know what Buddha-nature is, it is easy to set to work; if you do not know Buddha-nature, you cannot avoid practicing blindly and refining wildly. Therefore the Mahāmudrā is not that there is a hand-seal and a mantra for us to practice, but that it first speaks of the view as the school, corrects knowing and seeing, and makes us know what Buddha-nature is.

Summing up the discussion above, I think everyone has now clarified why the insentient is the sentient, why all insentient things are Buddha, and the question of “sentient and insentient alike perfect the wisdom of the Buddha.” If you truly understand and are clear about “sentient and insentient alike perfect the wisdom of the Buddha,” then if someone asks you what the Buddha is, you will not be struck dumb and at a loss — you need only casually bring up any one thing. Above and below heaven, above the sun and below the moon, inside the window and outside it, bright flowers and dark willows and so on — these insentient things are all Buddha! Picked up at random, each becomes a wondrous truth — how very convenient.

Above we have spoken of the insentient preaching the Dharma — how does the insentient preach? We have set out one layer of principle: the Dharma that has words to speak and the Dharma that has sound to hear are not the true Dharma. The true Dharma is without speech: “the path of language is cut off, the place of mental activity is extinguished” — that is, words cannot reach it and thought cannot think it; any Dharma with words and speech is not the true Dharma. Though we cannot hear the insentient preaching the Dharma, it is precisely preaching, because the great sound is rare in its sound. No-speaking is true speaking and no-hearing is true hearing; to hear a sound is not the true Dharma. Hence it is said: “If you listen with the ear, you will never grasp it; hearing the sound at the eye — only then do you know.” You may have a doubt in your mind: since no sound is heard, how can it be said that the insentient is preaching the Dharma? Because the truly wondrous and profound meaning cannot be expressed in words; it can only be understood by the mind and known by the spirit. If you abide in speech, you will not grasp the true meaning; hence “If you listen with the ear, you will never grasp it” — do not abide in sound! The wondrous meaning cannot be heard: “hearing the sound at the eye — only then do you know.” Why? Because this insentient preaching of the Dharma is a subtle and wondrous spiritual state in which, as a scene stirs feeling and the mind comprehends, one hears in no-hearing and the mind opens and the meaning is understood. When practice and inquiry reach the place where there is no speaking, no hearing, and no arising of delusive thought, you can be stirred by the scene and grasp the profound meaning within. Just as Dongshan asked his two masters whether they could hear the insentient preaching the Dharma, and both masters answered alike: “If I heard it, you would not hear me expound the Dharma.” The meaning is that true hearing is no-hearing; if I could hear it, I would be clinging to marks, and clinging to marks I would have no qualification to expound the Dharma and could not expound it for you. This layer of meaning was spoken last time, and we may add a little more. The true dharmakāya of all Buddhas neither speaks nor hears; the reward-body and transformation-body are not the true Buddha, for they speak and hear — hence “the reward and transformation bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they speakers of the Dharma.” If they speak and hear, do they still cling to speech? Just as I have said. If I had hearing, I would be the same as all Buddhas; I would be all Buddhas. The true dharmakāya of all Buddhas is without speech, so I could not expound the Dharma here; and if I could expound the Dharma, then I would not be the same as all Buddhas — this is another layer of meaning. We ordinary beings cling to marks at every moment: whatever the eye sees or the ear hears, we go on to discriminate good and bad, beautiful and ugly by our own views. One who has truly seen the nature, amid all sounds and forms, sees without seeing and hears without hearing. If you abide in the dust of sound or abide in marks of form, then you become an ordinary being. So it is said: if I heard it, I could not expound the Dharma for you. If I heard it I would be clinging to marks; clinging to marks, would I still be qualified to expound the Dharma for you? I could not. Below I shall sum up several points of meaning hidden in the Patriarch's words:

First point: if I heard it, I would be clinging to the dust of sound, have something to abide in, subject and object opposed, and my Dharma-view not removed; then I would not be a person of the Way and would have no qualification to expound the Dharma.
Second point: if I heard it, I would be the same as the insentient; and the insentient takes not speaking as true speaking, having no words — and then you could not hear me expound the Dharma.

Third point: if I heard it, I would be equal to the sages; but the reward-body and transformation-body of the sages are not true, nor are they speakers of the Dharma. The true dharmakāya of the sages neither speaks nor hears; and my speaking to you now is only a provisional means of drawing you in.

In speaking of these principles I want you all to understand that form and sound are both unobtainable, and that at every moment one should empty and purify one's mind and care for the true mind. Without caring for the true mind, one cannot attain the Way. To care for the true mind, one must first have right knowing and seeing and see the true mind, the intrinsic nature. Why is this so? We can verify it by the Chan school. Someone may ask: the Ganges Mahāmudrā that we are expounding is a tantric teaching — how is it verified by the Chan public cases of the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp? Because what the tantric teachings say is exactly the same as Chan and the Pure Land school, without the slightest difference. In all the schools and sects of the Buddhadharma, though the names and terms differ, the supreme principle is one and the same. Hence the Pure Land is the tantra, the tantra is Chan, and Chan is the Pure Land; all are the methods of attaining the Way spoken by the Buddha, only the tools used differ, and the fruition of the Way attained is without a second difference. The Ganges Mahāmudrā is the supreme tantric method of the tantric school and is very close to Chan, and so it is necessary to verify it by the principles of Chan. Among the five houses of Chan, what the Caodong house teaches corresponds most closely to the tantric teachings. The Caodong house speaks of the five positions of lord and minister, of five positions, to bring us from the ordinary being's knowing and seeing to the opening of the Buddha's knowing and seeing. Opening the Buddha's knowing and seeing is the stage of seeing the Way; beyond it is the stage of cultivating the Way; and after the stage of cultivating the Way comes the stage of realizing the Way, the realization of the fruition of Buddhahood. The five positions have three gradual stages — the stage of seeing the Way, the stage of cultivating the Way, and the stage of realizing the Way — the same as what the Mahāmudrā teaches; and the Mahāmudrā too begins with the stage of seeing the Way.

How does the Caodong house see the Way? It speaks of the primary position and the secondary position: the primary position represents substance, emptiness and principle; the secondary position represents function, form and affairs.

blocks.text: 3. The Five Positions of Lord and Minister in the Caodong House

inline.s: The first position: “The mid-primary within the secondary. Before the moon is bright in the third watch of the night, do not wonder that meeting you do not know each other; faintly you still cherish an old grudge.” — This is the position of the ordinary being. The ordinary being is like that moonless night “before the moon is bright in the third watch of the night,” pitch dark. Why? Because he does not know what Buddha-nature is; he recognizes only outer forms and marks, and covered by ignorance, his mind is pitch dark. “Do not wonder that meeting you do not know each other”: we are all within Buddha-nature at every moment and meet Buddha-nature at every moment, and yet we do not know it. In our eating, drinking, rising, resting and daily affairs, if Buddha-nature did not function, how could we move? When we get up in the morning and wash our face, brush our teeth, go out into the street, buy vegetables, go to work and do our jobs — who is doing this? Who is it? We may ask ourselves as the Chan school asks, “Who is it that recites the Buddha-name?” Tell me, if it is not the intrinsic nature, what is it? Since it is the intrinsic nature, why do we not know it when we meet it? Do not complain that the intrinsic nature is hard to know: in truth it is because we cling to marks, because of ignorance, because we lack wisdom! Ignorance is the dark night, and in the long long night, how can meeting lead to knowing? “Faintly you still cherish an old grudge”: faintly means not clearly. The habit of clinging that we ordinarily have works its mischief faintly there; we only want to grasp and seek and cling outside and are unwilling to turn the light around and see who it is that can move, who it is that can function. If you can turn the light around — who is this? — then you know it. So the mid-primary within the secondary means that we are originally on the primary position of the principle-substance, Buddha-nature, but without knowing or perceiving it we fall onto the secondary position and cling to affairs and marks there. The primary position is the principle-substance, the secondary position is form and mark; the primary is emptiness, the secondary is existence. Emptiness and existence, principle and affairs, substance and mark are all relative; there is secondary within primary, and one clings to the secondary position. Among the five houses of Chan the methods of receiving people differ, but what the Caodong house teaches is easy to understand. This is the first position — the position of the ordinary being, not knowing Buddha-nature.

The second position: “The mid-secondary within the primary. The belated old woman meets the ancient mirror; distinctly face to face there is no other truth; do not go on being confused about your head and taking the shadow for it.” — The stage of seeing the Way. Here, in the daily affairs of the secondary position, the principle-substance appears: that is, in dressing and eating one realizes at every moment that it is my Buddha-nature that is functioning, and one sees the Way — the stage of seeing the Way.

Earlier we spoke of pitch darkness; now it is bright. “Belated dawn” means daybreak, the sky about to be light, sunlight appearing. “Old woman” is very cleverly put — what does the old woman mean? “Old woman” means white hair; the sky is about to be light, and so white appears. “Meets the ancient mirror” is looking in a mirror; a mirror is bright and shining, a metaphor for there being light. The old woman meets the ancient mirror, the sky breaks, the light appears, and the cultivator reaches this dawn light and sees his own intrinsic nature; hence “the belated old woman meets the ancient mirror.” “Distinctly face to face there is no other truth”: the shadow in the mirror appears. Distinctly means perfectly clear; face to face means face to face. You meet the shadow in the mirror face to face; the shadow appearing in the mirror is you, you are the mirror — apart from this shadow is there any other truth? Apart from this shadow there is nothing more; hence “distinctly face to face there is no other truth.” When Lingyun opened his door and saw a whole hillside of blossoming peach trees, he suddenly awakened greatly: oh — if it is not my nature manifesting this mark, who manifests it? Apart from my nature, where could one see these peach blossoms? And conversely, apart from the shadow of the peach blossoms, where could my nature-mirror be manifested? So he turned the light around for a glance, knew this “distinctly face to face no other truth,” and saw the intrinsic nature! Again, Patriarch Dongshan awakened while crossing a river when he saw his own shadow. At that time he had asked about the insentient preaching the Dharma, and though his master told him and he had some awakening, he was not yet thoroughly clear and still had doubts. One day, as he was about to cross a river, he bent down to roll up his trouser legs and saw his own shadow appear in the water — “oh —!” — and only then did he awaken greatly, and he made a verse: “Above all, do not seek it from another; / Far, far away it is estranged from me. / Now I go alone on my way, / And everywhere I meet with it. / It now is precisely I; / I now am not it. / One must understand it just so / To be in accord with thusness.” What does this verse mean? “Above all, do not seek it from another”: in studying the Dharma and cultivating the Way we must not chase outward, must not seek it from others; only what one awakens to oneself is real. For example, when we who recite the Buddha-name recite Amitābha and pray to Amitābha in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — “come and pull me, come and pull me” — that is seeking it from another, and that is wrong. Hence Master Lianchi said that Buddha-recitation is “calling the master of the house to wake, sound by sound.” Buddha-recitation is waking our own master of the house, not letting him be dazed, not letting him sleep, not clinging to marks — be clear and awake! All phenomena are shadows in the mind; do not cling to marks! Our knowing-nature is Buddha-nature, is Amitābha! To seek it from another is to grasp outward. To pray outward for Amitābha to come and pull you is a mistake. Amitābha is one who practices great loving-kindness without conditions, receiving everyone and saving everyone; but he does not pull you — he shines light on you and receives you with light, and you need only enter that light. To want Amitābha to come and pull you will not do. Hence Chan Master Yongming Shou said: “When the cultivator's pure karma has ripened, his mind-ground is pure, and he is in accord with the Buddha, then he sees the Buddha appear before him and receive him to birth in the West. Though the Buddha appears before him, in truth he neither comes nor goes. Like the moon in the sky: in a thousand rivers and ten thousand waters it appears at once, yet the moon is in truth undivided. The mind is like the water: if the mind is impure, it is like turbid water, and no shadow appears. Therefore for one whose mind is inverted and confused, though the Buddha shines light to receive him, he is like one born blind who cannot see the sun.” The Buddha is like the moon in the sky and the mind that recites the Buddha-name is the water: if the water is pure, the moon's shadow appears in the water and the Buddha's image appears in your mind; if the mind that recites is impure, though the moon shines on you all the same, your mind is turbid foul water, and the moon's shadow cannot appear and Amitābha is not seen. Hence “above all, do not seek it from another”! If you look outward and seek outward, then “far, far away it is estranged from me” — to seek outside the mind puts you a hundred and eight thousand miles from Buddha-nature. Buddha-nature is nowhere else: it is shining at your face! Who is it that sees things? Who is it that hears sounds? Who is it that smells fragrance and stench? Who is it that speaks? Who is it that moves? What is this if not my Buddha-nature? Why do you seek it from another? “Now I go alone on my way”: now, whatever the time or place, I neither grasp nor reject outward things; all is “alone,” absolute, and I see no counterpart and no relativity. The absolute true mind is “alone,” absolute, without a single thing, without relativity. As when Emperor Wu of Liang asked, “What is the supreme meaning of the holy truth?” and Patriarch Bodhidharma answered, “Vast and empty, nothing holy.” Emperor Wu asked again, “Who is it that stands before me?” and the Patriarch answered, “I do not know.” Why did he not know? In relativity you know me and I know you; I am one alone — the absolute true mind. Being absolute, who knows whom? In the absolute true mind, to speak of knowing or not knowing is to speak in terms of two ends. If you can be like this, then “everywhere I meet with it”: at all times and in all places this absolute true mind can appear, and at all times and in all places you can see the true suchness of the intrinsic nature. “It now is precisely I”: “it” is the shadow. Mountains and rivers, the great earth, sun, moon and stars, all things whatsoever are nothing but my shadows, all are my manifestations. But “I now am not it”: this dharmakāya of mine is without marks; though the shadows are all my manifestations, I am not the shadows. That is, though all these marks are nothing but me, I am not all these marks, because the dharmakāya is without marks. Even if you took away all marks altogether, since none of them is me, it would be no loss to me. Therefore do not cling to marks: all marks are unobtainable, and one should not establish a single dharma. “One must understand it just so to be in accord with thusness.” Cultivators of the Way should understand it in this way; then the true mind can abide forever, can accord with thusness that does not move, and cannot be swayed by any object or circumstance. There is no place where my true mind is absent — it follows like a shadow — so at every moment we should not seek outward. To recite the Buddha-name is to be mindful of one's own mind; to recite Amitābha is to wake one's own mind, not to cling to marks. “The belated old woman meets the ancient mirror; distinctly face to face there is no other truth” — this is you! Apart from it, seek elsewhere and it cannot be found; it is gone. Therefore we have again and again pointed out to you all that this true mind, this awakened nature, is me, and apart from it there is nothing at all. If you think that this, which lacks the five superknowledges of the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of others' minds and the superknowledges of travel, is not the true mind, the awakened nature, then you are mistaken. For though through instruction you recognize this wondrous luminous substance — the true mind, the awakened nature — your delusive thoughts and clinging habits accumulated over many lives and many kalpas are very many and are not yet removed; how could you suddenly produce superknowledges? It is like a mirror covered with a thick layer of dust: how can it reflect? You must wipe and polish it until it is bright, and then it can illumine. But first you must have the mirror; if you do not have the mirror, what will you wipe and polish? So you must first, through instruction, recognize the wondrous luminous substance, and only then can you wipe and polish it. Wiping and polishing means that amid all sounds and forms, in all activities, you do not cling to marks, do not follow circumstances, but at every moment turn the light around. Let me repeat: only when you recognize the true mind and keep it, preserving it as it is, can you attain; otherwise, however you wipe and polish, it is all useless. Master Guifeng said: “What enters by the door is not the family treasure.” You must know it for yourself and then preserve it, and after a long time it is thorough. Today we have spoken of the first and second positions, the positions of the ordinary being and of seeing the Way.

In learning the Buddhadharma and cultivating the Dharma, the first thing is to recognize the intrinsic nature and affirm that this which can speak and can act is our true mind; then our feet stand firm and we have no doubt at all, and afterwards we care for it well, develop and magnify it, and realize the holy fruit. The Mahāmudrā is precisely this: first affirm Buddha-nature, then begin to practice. If this point cannot be affirmed, afterwards there is no way to begin, and the practice cannot succeed. Hence Patriarch Dongshan said well: “Distinctly face to face there is no other truth”! Apart from this shadow, seek again and it is gone. Buddha-nature is our capacity to give rise to knowing, the capacity that knows cold and warmth, cloud and clear, fullness and hunger, pain and itch; you must care for it at every moment.

The last line, “Do not go on being confused about your head and taking the shadow for it,” means: do not go on being deluded yourselves, do not go on chasing shadows. “Confused about the head and taking the shadow” is an example the Buddha gave in the Śūraṅgama Sutra. The Buddha said that in the city of Śrāvastī there was a man, Yajñadatta, who one day took a mirror and looked at himself, and saw in the mirror a made-up theatrical face, but did not see his own original face, and mistook it for a monster; so terrified that he ran about for no reason, he went out to look for his head. In fact his head was still on his shoulders and had not been lost. This is a simile to urge us not to be deluded by outer marks and mistake our original face. “Still taking the shadow”: you are still, at every moment, taking the shadow; but in truth that shadow is an illusory mark manifested by you — why take the false for the true? Women find it hardest to let go of their children and hang them on their minds all day long. And men? The young love girlfriends, the old love banknotes. Confucius said well: “In youth, when the blood and vital force are not yet settled, the thing to guard against is lust... and when old, when the blood and vital force have declined, the thing to guard against is acquisitiveness.” These are all the greed of taking shadows! Do not take shadows; let go. “Do not go on being confused about your head and taking the shadow for it”: amid the ten thousand false marks — the secondary — recognize and take up the true mind — the primary — and no longer be deluded by shadows. This is the second position, the mid-secondary within the primary — the stage of seeing the Way.

The third position: “The mid-primary come forth. Within nothing there is a road out of the dust; if only one can avoid touching the present taboo, one surpasses the tongue-cutting talent of former dynasties.” — The stage of cultivating the Way. if only one can avoid touching the present taboo, one surpasses the tongue-cutting talent of former dynasties.” — The stage of cultivating the Way.

Above we spoke of the stage of seeing the Way.
