blocks.text: 6. Not Knowing the Self-nature, Practice Is of No Benefit

inline.s: If you do not know your own wondrous mind, do not have right knowing and seeing, and do not know to cultivate from Buddha-nature but cling to marks and seek outward, then you have not left the functioning of the deluded mind; that is a wrong view of doing, and it is as far from the “Way of the self-nature’s great perfection” as the wind from the ox, and you will not obtain the “uncreated wheel of light.” The self-nature’s great perfection means that Buddha-nature is inherently complete and originally perfect, not obtained by grasping nor produced by cultivation. The uncreated wheel of light means that Buddha-nature is originally infinite in light, illumining the lands of the ten directions, complete in all wondrous functions, able to produce ten thousand transformations. The wheel of light is not produced by cultivation but is inherent in the self-mind. Hence it is said: “The Way is not a matter of cultivation but of awakening.” To awaken to the Way is to wake up, to understand, to enter the true mind, and to restore the original. That is, in practice, at the place where a thought is cut off, with a “ho” — you realize the original truth. After awakening, is cultivation needed? It is! Because the two clingings to self and dharma since beginningless time are still there, and one cannot yet develop great spiritual function; these two clingings must be exhausted before one can thoroughly realize the source. Then how shall one cultivate? That depends on the weight of each person’s habits, and different methods are used; but the best is the no-cultivation of non-doing, using the method of watching over. The Mahāmudrā method is: when a delusive thought arises, cry “Pei!”, cut it off, and thereby protect the true mind. But we may also use other methods, such as reciting the Buddha-name or holding mantras. When a delusive thought arises, recite Amitābha, or hold a mantra, do not follow the delusive thought, transform it, and you can equally protect the true mind. Or again, when a delusive thought arises, become alert and let all dissolve into emptiness, and the delusive thought subsides. So to obtain the “uncreated wheel of light,” one must first clearly realize this wondrous luminous true mind. If one does not understand what the true mind is, one cannot obtain it.

The view as the school is right knowing and right seeing: under the influence of right knowing and seeing, one recognizes the intrinsic nature. If you do not yet recognize the intrinsic nature, then “though you cultivate, you have no ground of preservation”; even if you practice diligently, you will not obtain the “uncreated wheel of light,” because you have no ground of preservation — you do not know what to preserve! That is, if you are still uncertain about the right knowing and seeing spoken of above, do not recognize the intrinsic nature, cannot stand firm on your feet, and are still in doubt, then what are you preserving? For example, if we have a small child, we must carefully look after him, protect him, not let him go hungry or cold, not let him fall, caring for him in every detail and bringing him up. If you have no child at all, then whom are you protecting?

Preservation is two stages of work: first preserving, then letting be. It is like a small child: first you must protect him, and when the child has grown up you let him be, let him stand on his own, do his own work, manage his own affairs, and you need not look after him. Preservation looks like only two words, but in practice it is a long road to walk! To do the work of preservation, one must first see the intrinsic nature; if you do not see the intrinsic nature, what are you preserving? And what is the intrinsic nature? Much has been said above: it is the nature that can now see and now hear; recognize it, do not doubt it, and care for it well. How to care for it? “It is not that one does not see, not that one does not hear,” but that “one is vividly aware of it, without clinging to seeing and hearing.” In daily life it is not that one does not look at things or listen to sounds, but that one does not discriminate good and bad, beautiful and ugly, and does not give rise to love and hate, acceptance and rejection. Though you look and though you listen, there is nothing in the mind — “vast and non-abiding”; that is “preserving.” When preservation has ripened, you no longer preserve: let it go, you may go anywhere, do anything at all, with not the slightest abiding — and so you reach the state of non-obstruction in all things and free and easy functioning. Concerning “non-obstruction in all things,” Chan Master Zhenjing Kewen has a verse: “Non-obstruction in all things, / Sovereign and free; / A pig’s head in the hand, / Pure precepts on the lips, / Thrown out of the brothel, / The wine debt unpaid, / At the crossroads, / Opening the cloth bag.” Holding a pig’s head in your hand, gnawing pig’s head meat, and reciting the precepts: no killing, no stealing, no sexual misconduct... I am a vegetarian — I have just come out of the brothel, ha ha ha! “Thrown out” means being driven out. A brothel is a house of prostitutes. When the money is spent in the brothel, the madam drives you out. Drunk and in debt, the tavern comes to dun you for the wine money, and you are too poor to pay. Just so slovenly, just so down and out, and thereby free and easy, without care or worry. Someone may ask: pig’s head in hand, pure precepts on the lips... not eating vegetarian — is that not breaking the precepts? Not at all! He has not eaten meat; he is a vegetarian. Why? His mind is empty, he does not cling to marks, and he has never felt that meat tastes good and so eaten more, or that vegetables taste bad and so eaten less. To be without love and hate, without grasping and rejecting, is to be a vegetarian. By contrast, some who eat vegetarian food cling to flavors: this dish tastes good, delicious; that dish tastes bad, unpalatable! Picking and choosing — that is as good as not being a vegetarian. If our mind is truly empty and pure, eating is as if not eating, and holding a pig’s head in the hand does not matter.

But then again, if you have not realized to this degree and you let yourself go like this, then you will “fall into hell as swift as an arrow”! Your mind has not truly become empty and pure, and “karma” sticks to you, entangles you, and will not let you pass. Here is such a public case: long ago there was a Chan master who loved beef, and he said, “Eating is not eating!” Was his mind empty and pure? No! It was only talk; his mind could not be emptied, and karmic obstacles stuck to him and demanded repayment. When this Chan master’s last breath did not come, he entered a cow’s womb and became a cow to repay the debt. One day a farmer led the cow out and met Chan Master Baozhigong. Zhigong looked: oh! Is this not Chan Master So-and-so? Did you not say, “Eating is not eating”? You should not have become a cow — how is it that you became a cow to repay a debt? The cow, tears streaming down its face, dashed itself to death. So unless one has truly reached the stage of emptiness and purity, to talk wild and big is to fall into hell. We are determined to realize the great Way; we should speak only according to the stage we have realized — no wild talk! To realize the stage of “non-obstruction in all things,” one must first have pure and correct views, clearly see the true mind, and then further remove deluded habits and enter non-doing. To cultivate while clinging to marks, to cultivate with doing — neither can realize “non-obstruction in all things.” Nowadays some people, with minds not empty and pure, vainly seek superknowledges — ruined! Not only can they not become Buddhas, they are in line to become demons! If you want superknowledges, the demon manifests superknowledges in your mind, changes into a Buddha’s form to show you, and you think it is the true Buddha, happily hold on to it, and the demon takes up residence in your mind. The demon king will even expand his influence, making you expound the Dharma and gather a host of demon sons and demon grandchildren. All this is because of clinging to marks; therefore we must not cling to marks, must not cultivate with doing.
“Therefore to verify and confirm the view as the school is foremost.”

This is the weightiest sentence. The view as the school is clearly seeing the intrinsic nature. The Ganges Mahāmudrā places the view as the school in the foremost position, and the Caodong house’s “five positions of lord and minister” highlights this too. The Linji house has the “three mysteries and three essentials,” and among them the first essential of the “mystery within the phrase” is to know one’s own mind and see one’s own nature, which highlights this as well.

One must first realize and see the intrinsic nature; only then can one manifest the “wisdom of self-abiding.” After awakening, preserve the intrinsic nature without losing it, practice diligently, and sweep away deluded habits. If in any favorable or adverse circumstance the mind is like still water, without the least deviation, then all superknowledges and wondrous functions come without seeking. “Abiding in one’s own intrinsic nature” means that it is inherent in the self-mind and naturally issues from the original mind. “Not sought from another” means it is not obtained by cultivating some dharma, nor given to us by Buddhas and bodhisattvas, still less manifested by some ghost or spirit possessing one. “Nor is it absent before and present now”: it is not that it did not exist before and exists only now, but that it has always existed. Someone asks: “You say it has always existed, so why do I not have it now?” Because your delusive thoughts and delusive habits are not yet exhausted! First you must recognize Buddha-nature and clearly awaken to the fact that this capacity to see and to hear is the intrinsic nature. Then care for it at every moment, do not cling to marks, do not run after circumstances. When preservation is complete and ripe and the mind is truly empty and pure, superknowledges will appear of themselves.

If it is not “abiding in one’s own mind” and not developed by oneself, then it has nothing to do with you: when the last breath does not come, none of the functions remain, and you do not even know where you are going. If you have done bad things, you will fall into hell — very dangerous! In Shanghai there were several so-called “possessors of superknowledges”; as death approached, the spirits attached to them left and went away, and then they not only had no superknowledges but suffered greatly in the body and, in mind, were tormented by guilt and the reproaches of conscience, crying only, “Pain! Suffering!” and falling into the three lower realms. We who practice the true Dharma should take warning!
Becoming familiar with the dharmakāya

In our practice we must let the mind be like a river, bending and turning as it goes. Have no subjective abiding at all; let all follow conditions and be free, without self-view and without obstruction. At all times flow on peacefully and freely like flowing water — this is how the work should be done. We ordinary beings are heavy with selfishness and full of delusive thoughts, and want everything to accord with our own wishes: “I want it this way, so it must be this way,” and otherwise the mind is afflicted; hence karmic obstacles are heavy and we cannot see the Way. Now that we practice the Way, we must change this habit of abiding and be able to follow conditions and things: bend where it bends, turn where it turns, and not stubbornly hold to our own views. For example, in our work, if we are promoted, we are promoted; if demoted, demoted — it does not matter. We must not be delighted by promotion or angered by demotion. Because everything is service to the people, not to oneself, one must be able to go up and to go down. Having learned the Buddhadharma, we know that all sounds, forms, goods and profits are like flowers in the sky and moons in water, not to be sought and not to be obtained, and the mind abides always in emptiness and stillness, without affliction; so every problem can be discussed, and every task can be taken up selflessly and pressed forward with courage. If everyone acted thus, giving up self for others, society would be at peace, the nation would flourish, and the country would be strong and prosperous. So learning Buddhism is of great benefit to the world and to people’s minds, and should truly be vigorously promoted.

When we do things, we should not care whether we succeed or fail, but only do our utmost: not delighted by success, not angered by failure, summing up experience, correcting mistakes, and pressing on with renewed effort. If one can make one’s thinking broad and open, without crookedness or selfishness, unmoved and unshaken, then one naturally realizes the original face of the dharmakāya. Likewise, one should not, merely because a thought arises, give rise to the notion that “the mind’s light is covered by dark clouds”; nor, when delusive thoughts subside, give rise to the notion of “having removed them.” For as soon as the thought of “leaving” and “emerging” arises, that is delusion upon delusion, and one is still clinging to something and cannot be liberated. The Mahāmudrā teaches action in non-doing, with no defilement at all, following conditions and being free at every moment; its work is a level higher and harder to do. If for the moment you cannot do it, you must do other work; this will be explained later.

Therefore we must be thus at every moment: when a thought comes, pay it no heed, do not press it down, do not run after it; follow conditions and be free, respond to the ten thousand opportunities without abiding — this is our dharmakāya’s own mark. Our own Dharma-nature is originally thus: it can produce wondrous function according to the opportunity, it is not dead and motionless. It responds with extraordinary speed, faster than light. The reason ordinary beings respond slowly is that they have many delusive thoughts; it is like the sun covered by dark clouds, so that its light cannot come forth and its function is thereby reduced. To develop superknowledges is simply that when delusive thoughts are exhausted the mind’s function comes fully into play. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is inherently complete with infinite superknowledges and wondrous functions. If only we can be mindless like a flowing river and let it be natural — as it is said, the fallen flower has intent, the flowing water has none — and thus at every moment be free and unconstrained, we can restore the dharmakāya’s own mark and greatly manifest superknowledges. The dharmakāya’s own mark is not the absence of a single thought, rigidly knowing nothing. It is lively, arising in function according to conditions, with boundless wondrous function. What is called no-thought does not mean that not one thought arises; it means that thoughts arise without abiding. Emptiness is existence and existence is emptiness!

Speaking of emptiness and existence: this matters greatly for studying Buddhism. Only when the relation of emptiness and existence is fully understood can one advance swiftly. Those who practice always say all is empty and one should not cling to existence, while ordinary beings in their affairs all cling to existence, so that emptiness and existence seem irreconcilable opposites. This is because people understand “emptiness” and “existence” differently. What ordinary beings call emptiness is that everything is nothing; what the Buddhadharma calls emptiness is only the absence of self-substance, not the absence of false marks. Hence “form itself is emptiness,” and it is not that one speaks of emptiness apart from false marks. The emptiness we speak of is not the ordinary being’s emptiness of total nothingness but the emptiness of not abiding in false marks, the emptiness in which “emptiness is existence, existence is emptiness, emptiness and existence are non-dual.” So no-thought is not the non-arising of a single thought but the arising of thoughts without following or abiding; this principle must be understood. Buddha-nature is truly empty, but it is not that it does not manifest, for when it functions it must manifest. If it were empty and had no marks, it would not be the self-nature. For where there is mind there must be marks; mind is marks and marks are mind, mind and marks being non-dual. As I said last time, there must be a shadow in a mirror, and without a shadow it is not a mirror; so Buddha-nature can certainly manifest form and mark, and without form and mark it could not be called Buddha-nature, for without wondrous function Buddha-nature would become dead emptiness, barren emptiness. But Buddha-nature is not barren emptiness: it is numinously clear and all-pervading, able to produce all wondrous functions and to manifest all kinds of form and mark; hence “the myriad phenomena are perfected within the mind.”

Speaking of this, let me tell you a story. In Zhenjiang there is a Jinshan Temple, and in the temple there is a treasure that guards the mountain. The treasure is Su Dongpo’s jade belt, made of square jades strung on gold thread. How did this jade belt remain in Jinshan Temple? Su Dongpo and the abbot of Jinshan Temple, Chan Master Foyin, were close friends. Su Dongpo wrote excellent poetry and was also a Buddhist practitioner, and he prided himself that his practice had reached the point of being unmoved by the eight winds. Chan Master Foyin wanted to test the depth of his practice, and deliberately belittled him: “Su Dongpo’s poems are not worth a dog’s fart.” Hearing this, Su Dongpo could not help but be greatly angered, and raising a punitive expedition, he crossed the river in a rage to confront Chan Master Foyin. Chan Master Foyin laughed: “A fine ‘unmoved by the eight winds’ — one fart blew you across the river.” This is a joke.

Once Su Dongpo came to Jinshan Temple to visit Chan Master Foyin. The Master was at that time in the Chan hall leading the assembly in sitting meditation, and it was the time of stillness when idlers should not enter. Su Dongpo knew the rule and sat waiting in the guest hall for Chan Master Foyin to come out. When that stick of incense was finished another was added, so he came out very late. Su Dongpo had waited a long time and was very impatient. When the incense was finished and the stillness ended, Chan Master Foyin came out: “Ah! Great Scholar Su, please sit, please sit.” Su Dongpo said: “Hey, you still tell me to sit! I want to sit on the head of you bald donkey!” They were good friends joking, calling the Master a “bald donkey.” Hearing this, the Master said: “Oh, you want to sit on this old monk’s head? Good, good, good. I have a question to ask you. If you can answer it, this old monk’s head is yours to sit on; if you cannot, then untie the jade belt from your waist and give it to us as a treasure to guard the mountain.” Su Dongpo laughed heartily: “Whatever question you like, I can answer ten for one; I have many wondrous interpretations and broad explanations.” Chan Master Foyin said: “Good. I ask you: the four great elements are originally empty, the five aggregates are not existent — where do you sit?” The meaning was: you want to sit on my head; my body is the four great elements and five aggregates, empty and non-existent — how will you sit? Su Dongpo thought: the four great elements are empty, the five aggregates originally do not exist, everything is nothing — then I fall into emptiness; where shall I sit? I cannot sit in empty space... He thought and thought, walked back and forth three times, and for the moment could not answer. Chan Master Foyin seized the chance and called the novice monk: “Come, untie his jade belt — he cannot answer.” And so Su Dongpo’s jade belt remained in Jinshan Temple as a treasure to guard the mountain. This is the public case of “empty yet existent, existent yet empty.” In fact this question is not hard to answer, for emptiness is not barren emptiness and existence is not real existence; emptiness does not obstruct existence and existence does not obstruct emptiness; emptiness is existence and existence is emptiness, mind is mark and mark is mind. So one may answer him: “True emptiness does not obstruct wondrous existence — I sit right on your false-mark head!” Or simply sit down on the chair and say: “Thus I sit!” Or raise one finger and say: “I sit right here!” Or again raise a finger and ask him: “Where do you sit?” These answers are picked up at random and need no racking of brains.

Someone asked the lecturer on the Diamond Sutra: “No mark of person, no mark of self — then who speaks and who hears?” This question looks very hard: with no person and no self, there is no speaking and no hearing — can one still expound and listen to the sutra here? In fact the Diamond Sutra is about breaking marks to see the nature; it does not belong to barren emptiness. Though things and marks are absent, Buddha-nature is not absent. One may answer him: “It speaks only of no marks, not of no person.” Our Buddha-nature is wondrous existence that is not existence, true emptiness that is not emptiness. If everyone makes clear the principle of emptiness and existence, existence and emptiness, and then goes further to preserve it closely and continuously at all times, not abiding in marks and not falling into emptiness, one can perfectly realize the great Way. Otherwise, as soon as we meet a circumstance or mark we stick to it and are not free — when will it ever end?

In the school there are many such public cases. In the time of Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty, a prime minister invited the elders of all schools and sects to hold an unveiling assembly — with nothing covered, each stating his own view, directly and revealing the intrinsic nature and perfectly realizing the great Way. A lecturer on the Avataṃsaka Sutra said: “In our teaching, becoming a Buddha requires three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas. But the school says that one shout or one blow can make one a Buddha, which does not accord at all with the Buddha’s teaching. Now I ask the great Chan masters present: if one shout of yours can penetrate the five teachings spoken of by the Avataṃsaka school, I will acknowledge that one blow or one shout can make one a Buddha; if it cannot penetrate the five teachings, then it is a demon’s teaching. Will one of you come forward and explain?” The Avataṃsaka school divides the Buddhadharma into five teachings: the Hīnayāna teaching, the elementary Mahāyāna teaching, the final Mahāyāna teaching, the sudden Mahāyāna teaching, and the perfect Mahāyāna teaching, with doctrines from shallow to deep and practice advancing step by step. Among the great Chan worthies present was Patriarch Yuanwu Keqin, over eighty years old, the master of Chan Master Dahui Zonggao. He looked with his eyes at the young Chan master Jingyin Cheng, over forty, and Chan Master Jingyin Cheng understood; he stepped forward and said to the Avataṃsaka lecturer: “Your question is not hard to answer; it is not worth the great patriarchs present explaining it to you — let me, a junior elder, explain it to you. Let us first settle the doctrines of the five teachings: the Hīnayāna teaching holds to existence — there is a Way to attain, a nirvāṇa to realize, a birth and death to end; the elementary Mahāyāna teaching speaks of emptiness; the final Mahāyāna teaching speaks of neither emptiness nor existence — neither empty nor existent; the sudden Mahāyāna teaching speaks of both emptiness and existence; the perfect Mahāyāna teaching speaks of neither emptiness nor existence, neither existence nor emptiness, perfectly interfused and unobstructed. Is that the meaning?” The Avataṃsaka lecturer said: “Yes!” Chan Master Jingyin Cheng gave a great shout, and asked the assembly: “Did you hear it?” The assembly said: “We heard it!” Cheng said: “If you heard it, that is existence! You have penetrated the Hīnayāna.” Emperor Huizong was at that time sitting among the assembly in plain clothes and a small cap; he had told the prime minister not to reveal him, so that he might listen well to how it was explained. After a while the sound died away, and Cheng asked again: “Now that you listen, is there still a sound?” The assembly said: “There is none!” Cheng said: “No sound is emptiness — you have penetrated the elementary teaching.” He said further: “Now there is none and just now there was — that is not emptiness; just now there was and now there is none — that is not existence. Is this not neither empty nor existent? You have penetrated the final teaching. Moreover, if there were not the existence of just now, what emptiness could be spoken of now? If there were not the emptiness of now, what existence of just now could be spoken of? When existence is spoken of, emptiness is within existence; when emptiness is spoken of, existence is within emptiness — is this not both empty and existent? You have penetrated the sudden teaching. And the perfect Mahāyāna teaching? My one shout is not used as one shout: though I shout, I have never shouted, and at every moment and in every place I do not cling to marks. Eating, I have not bitten a single grain of rice; wearing clothes, I have not hung on a single thread. Though work is busy, it is as if I had never worked. This is the essential meaning of the Diamond Sutra’s ‘give rise to the mind that abides nowhere’: when existence is spoken of, not a hair is established; when emptiness is spoken of, it pervades the sand-grain worlds; not abiding in emptiness or existence, perfectly interfused and unobstructed — this is the supreme perfect Mahāyāna teaching, the highest state spoken of in the Avataṃsaka Sutra, the Dharma-realm of non-obstruction in all things. This is also the essence of the Chan school.” When the assembly heard this, all were convinced and praised, and Emperor Huizong nodded without cease. The Buddhadharma is truly the most sublime religion and the best philosophy of life. If we can believe, accept and practice it, what affliction of success and failure, gain and loss can remain? The Ganges Mahāmudrā teaches the supreme Buddhadharma; since we have most fortunately heard this Dharma, we should practice according to the teaching, making the mind at every moment like a river, functioning freely without abiding, and only then can we realize the dharmakāya’s own mark.

When a thought arises in the mind, one should know that this is the functioning of wisdom, the wondrous function of Dharma-nature. This is so not only when watching over but at all times. Therefore when one is lax and does not practice, Dharma-nature does not decrease; when one diligently accumulates practice, Dharma-nature does not increase. Dharma-nature itself neither increases nor decreases.

Many of us, in studying Buddhism and doing the work, tend to press thoughts down so they do not arise, thinking that to sit for ten days or half a month, or even ten or eight years, without a single thought arising is good practice. They do not know that cultivating dead samādhi thus brings no true benefit and cannot leave the three realms; it only suppresses for a time, and once it stirs and delusive thoughts arise they are worse than before. And even if it does not stir, what use is sitting there dead? After long dead samādhi one turns into earth, wood, metal and stone. True practice must be lively, tempering oneself amid affairs and circumstances, knowing that where a thought arises is the wondrous function of the intrinsic nature, and not clinging to marks — then wisdom grows daily. We must practice to become living Buddhas, not dead Buddhas; we must produce all kinds of wondrous function and benefit sentient beings — only thus is there value. Not sitting there dead and motionless — would that not make one a clay bodhisattva?

As said before, after seeing the intrinsic nature one must diligently remove habits amid affairs and circumstances. Watching over is the best method for removing habits. Watching over is the wondrous function of Buddha-nature! It is wondrous function not only when watching over but at all times. For example, wandering in mountains and playing in water, visiting relatives and friends, watching plays and dancing are all wondrous function. It is not that one may not watch a play, but one must not be watched by the play, nor turned by its plot. If while watching you repeatedly give rise to joy, anger, sorrow and pleasure along with the play’s partings and reunions, and afterwards cannot forget it and brood over it, your mind always turning with the plot — this person so good, that person so bad — that is called being watched by the play; how can that do? Watching a play can also be used to train the mind, to see whether this mind can be turned. If you can reach “like a wooden man watching flowers and birds,” that is good practice. But this is not to say that one does not know the good and bad people in the play, or does not know the plot. If one knew nothing at all, would that not be a pool of dead water? It is not that one does not know, but that one does not discriminate and choose, and is not moved by the play’s plot. Watching yet not watching, not watching yet watching, without the least abiding. “The affairs of the world are after all only a play”: we cannot let go of this or that, yet all of it is as false as a play! When the last breath does not come, the play is over — why cling to it?

In our practice, if we work diligently, the dharmakāya does not increase by a fraction; if we are lax, the dharmakāya does not decrease by a fraction. In other words, when we become Buddhas the dharmakāya does not increase a fraction, and as sentient beings it does not decrease a fraction; ascending to heaven it does not increase, descending to hell it does not decrease. It has no birth or death, no coming or going, and endures through all ages unchanging. In America a “living Buddha” named Lu Sheng-yen said: “By practice, Buddha-nature (the heavenly mind) ascends to heaven, and the bad, evil mind descends to the earth.” One ascends and one descends, one true mind split into two — that is truly terrible! Some Dharma masters say in expounding the sutras: “If we do bad things, the deluded mind that does bad things falls into hell, and the true mind ascends to heaven.” This too splits true and deluded into two minds. They do not know that the true mind (Buddha-nature) and the deluded mind are originally one body: the deluded mind is the true mind and the true mind is the deluded mind. For example, water (the true mind) gives rise to waves (the deluded mind): the waves are water and the water is the waves — how can there be two? Someone asks: “If there are not two, why do people speak of three souls and seven spirits? Are there not ten?” If it were really so, would a person not become ten? Not at all! What is called “soul” belongs to yang and is the bright, selfless, upright qi; what is called “spirit” belongs to yin and is the dark, defiled, evil thought. “Three souls and seven spirits” means that a person’s bright element is small, only three parts, while the dark, unseemly things are many, seven parts. It is not that a person is divided into ten things. If we drive out all seven parts of dark, evil mind and turn them all into light, we attain the Way. Thus Patriarch Lü Chunyang was called “pure yang” because his “spirits” were all transformed, the darkness all turned to light, and he attained the immortal Way. Therefore the true mind and the deluded mind are not two things. When you fall into hell, the true mind falls into hell with you, but its light does not decrease, nor is it defiled, nor does it suffer. It is like a pearl wrapped in mud: the pearl’s light does not decrease. When you ascend to heaven, it is not glad, and its light does not increase. Our self-nature at every moment is neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither coming nor going, neither moving nor shaking, neither arising nor ceasing.

The reason we have feelings of greed, anger, affliction, suffering and pleasure is that they are all the natural wondrous function of the dharmakāya. If there were no dharmakāya, these feelings could not arise. But this changing of different emotions — now joy, now sorrow and affliction — is all the mischief of the three poisons of greed, anger and delusion. Meeting with what we dislike we are afflicted; seeking and not obtaining we are angry; unable to fulfill our wishes we are grieved and resentful; fulfilling our desires we are delighted and happy. These feelings are all empty and without self-nature, all delusive thoughts arising toward objects. As it is said, “The ten thousand dharmas are originally at leisure; only people make trouble for themselves” — and this is because of fundamental ignorance. Speaking of ignorance, all who practice fear it: it is this thing that harms people and makes us turn in the six realms! If it were not there, we would long ago have become Buddhas! But do not fear it: ignorance is not really existent, it is only a delusive thought, an illusion, and as soon as we awaken we illumine through it. Because it is not a really existent thing, it cannot be broken with any object. One need only awaken to the fact that greed, anger, delusion, pride and doubt are all deluded feelings arising from clinging to objects and sticking to the mind, all ignorance and delusive thought, inherently just so and utterly non-existent. “Just so” means “originally thus, not deliberately contrived.” When we understand this wondrous principle, all suffering, pleasure and affliction dissolve as soon as we awaken. As the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Know the illusory and at once you are free, without using any device; freedom from the illusory is awakening, and there are no stages.” We commonly say “karmic obstacles are deep and heavy” — what are karmic obstacles? Karmic obstacles are your clinging to marks. If you do not cling to marks, there is no affliction at all, and where would karmic obstacles come from? All feelings of suffering and pleasure are like dreams in sleep: in the dream, bad dreams and good dreams are perfectly there, but once you wake there is nothing. So if we can wake up sharply, let everything go, and not cling to marks, we obtain the dharmakāya’s wondrous function. The dharmakāya’s wondrous function is not hard: we need only be clear and awake at every moment and not abide in marks at every moment.

Someone says: “Ah! Chan practice and tantra are hard; reciting the Buddha-name and seeking birth in the West is easy!” In fact he is mistaken: Buddha-recitation, Chan practice and tantra are all the same, with no distinction of hard and easy; one simply chooses a method suited to oneself according to one’s differing capacities. Buddha-recitation uses the Buddha-name to sweep the accumulated dirt from one’s mind-ground and, by holding the name, to wake oneself up. Master Lianchi said that Buddha-recitation is “calling the master of the house to wake, sound by sound.” That is, with each sound one devoutly recites the holy name and wakes one’s own intrinsic nature, not abiding in marks and not sticking to objects, thereby personally seeing Buddha-nature and, at the end of life, being born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Chan practice is the same: at every moment tend the huatou, watching where delusive thoughts come from. As soon as a thought arises, ask it: where do you come from? A blow straight to the head. This delusive thought originally does not exist; it is a false illusion, and one blow and it is gone. This is the same as Buddha-recitation: both are to exhaust delusive thought and thereby personally realize the original. But some say they are different: they say Buddha-recitation has Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva and all the bodhisattvas of the Lotus Pool assembly to receive one, so that one is born in the West and transcends the three realms horizontally, while Chan practice cannot. In fact they are also mistaken: receiving and horizontal transcendence do exist, but receiving and horizontal transcendence do not mean pulling you away. Chan Master Yongming Shou said very clearly: the Buddha is like the moon in the sky and the mind is like a basin of water; only when the mind is pure can the moon’s shadow appear; if the mind is impure — foul water — then though the moon is in the sky (though the Buddha shines light on you, you cannot see it), the shadow cannot appear, and you cannot be born in the West. Great Master Hanshan said that in reciting the Buddha-name one must recite to the point of power, cutting off the root of love, and only then is there hope of birth in the West. The root of love is the love-emotion of ignorance and deluded movement; it is the root of birth and death, and if it is not cut off the mind is like foul water in which the moon’s shadow cannot appear. It is not that the Buddha does not come to receive you and does not shine light on you; it is only that you yourself cannot see, like a blind person who cannot see the sun. Moreover, for one who practices Chan, when the mind-ground is empty and pure, that is the Pure Land. For mind is the land and the land is the mind. The Buddha said: “If you wish to purify the land, first purify the mind; as the mind is purified, the Buddha-land is purified.” Only when the mind is pure is the Buddha-land pure, and then if you vow to be born in the West, you will certainly receive Amitābha Buddha’s compassionate reception and be born there. Amitābha is not like us ordinary beings, who have feelings of love and hate: if you have formed a good connection with me, I receive you; if you have not, I pay you no heed. Buddhas and bodhisattvas practice great loving-kindness without conditions and have no such inferior view: if you have not formed a connection with me, then I will form one with you and compassionately receive you. In tantric terms, whether you recite the Buddha-name or practice other methods, at the end of your life Amitābha shines light on you and receives you to birth in the West. And not only practitioners: even non-practitioners and evildoers he also shines on and receives. Only these evildoers, heavy with karmic obstacles, cannot see the Buddha-light, or seeing it so intense are frightened and flee, and have no fortune to be born in the West. The Amitābha Sutra says: “One cannot be born in that land with few roots of goodness, blessings, and causes.” Roots of goodness, blessings, and causes — not one of the three may be lacking. To be born in the West one must be complete in roots of goodness, blessings and causes; it is not something to be had by casually reciting a couple of “Amitābha.”

All you bodhisattvas, we must truly apply effort and completely settle the deluded mind before we can attain the Way! The Mahāmudrā teaches the mind-ground Dharma-gate. The one true Dharma-realm — the Lotus Treasury world — is the Mahāmudrā. The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is within this Mahāmudrā and does not go outside it. The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss’s “land of coexistence of sages and ordinary beings” is on the thirteenth level of this Mahāmudrā, and the “land of real reward and adornment” is the twentieth level of the Lotus Treasury world. Our Sahā world is also the thirteenth level, parallel to the West’s “land of coexistence of sages and ordinary beings.” The Buddha said: “West of here, past a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands, there is a world called Ultimate Bliss.” That is, going west from here is the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss’s “land of coexistence of sages and ordinary beings.” If only we believe deeply without doubt, do all good deeds, and vow and transfer the merit toward birth there, we can all go, and the Buddhas and bodhisattvas will not refuse us. It is not that one cannot go without reciting Amitābha’s holy name. Someone says: “I recite the Buddha-name only a little; I fear I cannot go.” That is wrong! Whether one is born in the West does not depend on how much one recites — this is not a business transaction — but on the quality of your recitation, whether your mind-ground is devout, whether your mind is pure. If your mind is truly pure, then at the end of life even one thought can bring birth in the West. If we can reflect that all form, sound, smell, taste, touch and dharmas are flowers in the sky and moons in water, not to be sought and not to be obtained, and let go of everything at once, and with a pure, undefiled mind recite one “Amitābha,” this one pure thought can be in accord with the Buddha and bring birth in the West — no need for ten thoughts, a hundred thoughts, a thousand or ten thousand thoughts. It depends on whether at the end of life you can be single-minded without confusion and clear in right thought. At the end of life, to be unconfused in mind, undistracted in intent, and clear in right thought — this is the practice of deeply attaining the Buddha-recitation samādhi! To bring the practice to this point depends on the diligent sweeping away of deluded habits now. So we must now apply effort, devoutly letting go, letting go, and letting go again, making the mind pure and undefiled, so that in the future we may surely win and be born in the West — this too is the dharmakāya’s wondrous function! We blend Chan, Pure Land and tantra into one furnace because they are originally one body. Do not divide them into tantra, Chan, Pure Land — they are originally one Buddha school!

blocks.text: 2. The Great Natural Abiding of Non-cultivation

inline.s: In all our actions at all times and in all places, there is the wondrous function of the true mind, and all forms are our own transformation bodies. We should follow all kinds of conditions in responding and acting, doing our utmost to benefit the people — this is called “natural free functioning.” If one does not understand and does not penetrate the principle of “natural free functioning,” one will certainly cling to objects and stick to the mind, and with insatiable greed, to satisfy one’s desires, delusive thoughts will fly in confusion, and one will bury a great living Buddha as an ordinary man or foolish woman. We practice the Dharma originally to see the nature and realize the Way, clinging to nothing. If one wants superknowledges, wants to obtain something, or prays to Buddhas and bodhisattvas for promotion and wealth, that runs counter to studying Buddhism. Now we need only be free and non-abiding at every moment, not adding knowing to any delusive state, and yet not like wood or stone, but vividly and distinctly responding to opportunities and following conditions — this is Buddha-work. We have said before: do not acknowledge this form-body as self, but take emptiness-and-stillness as the substance; do not acknowledge delusive thoughts, but take numinous knowing as the mind. Cultivating by the mind-ground Dharma-gate is like using rice to cook a meal: it will certainly become a meal. If one does not practice thus, it is like boiling sand to make a meal: however much effort is spent, no meal is made. Once we understand that this pure, undefiled, vividly distinct numinous knowing mind is the Buddha, we no longer cling to marks but freely and naturally serve the people, tempering ourselves amid affairs and circumstances, exhausting deluded habits, and perfecting the fruition of Buddhahood. Otherwise delusive thoughts will fly in confusion, one falls of oneself into the ordinary and foolish, and birth and death are not ended. We ordinary beings have been accustomed to clinging to marks for many lives and kalpas, and cannot change all at once: not only do we pick and choose in food, drink and daily life, but in practicing the Dharma too we pick and choose without cease. One says: “The Pure Land school is good and reliable; Chan is dangerous and unreliable.” Another says: “Tantra is good.” Another says: “Tantra is not good either — tantra is full of demonic air.” Oh, this is good, that is bad — all blind men feeling an elephant, falsely discriminating and talking nonsense. They do not know that the Dharma spoken by the Buddha is equal, equal, and again equal; it is only that different Dharma-gates are taught according to people’s differing capacities — this is called “giving medicine according to the illness.” It is like eating: if you like sweet food, take sweet food; if you like sour food, take sour food. If one who loves sour says sweet food is bad, and one who loves sweet says sour food is bad; if those who recite the Buddha-name say Chan is dangerous (in fact Chan is not dangerous), and those who practice Chan say tantra has demonic air (in fact tantra has no demonic air) — all this is over-weighting one’s own preference, falsely discriminating, and not only brings affliction on oneself but invisibly incurs the offense of slandering the Dharma. Whichever school you like, practice that school; do not say other schools are bad — any one school is the same. You say Chan is hard, but practicing other schools is not easy either; you say Buddha-recitation is easy, but practicing other schools is not hard either.

Pang the layman said: “Hard, hard, hard — ten loads of sesame oil spread on a tree.” This speaks of the beginner who does not understand the key to practice, and so it is very hard, like “a slippery fish climbing a slick pole”: the fish’s scales are slimy and slippery — to climb that oiled bamboo pole, how easy is that! But once it is pointed out, it turns out that this which can speak, can act, can weep, can laugh is our own self-nature; it shines at our face all day long, hiding nothing, needing no seeking and no praying — only let everything go and that is it. As it is said, “Wearing out iron shoes you search in vain; what you get costs not a bit of effort.” So Mother Pang took up the words: “Easy, easy, easy — on the tips of the hundred grasses is the meaning of the coming from the West.” Not hard at all — awakening to Chan is very easy. “On the tips of the hundred grasses” means on the tip of anything at all; “on the tip” means looking apart from marks, not looking downward and clinging to marks. The capacity to see things apart from marks is the wondrous function of the self-nature! Is that not very easy? So in our practice we should not divide into schools and sects, saying this is hard and that is easy; we need only recognize at every moment this true mind that is apart from marks and vividly distinct, and not acknowledge shadows — shadows cannot be grasped. At this point, though the principle is clear, the habit of abiding in marks from many lives and kalpas will still intrude. Master Guifeng said: “Deluded clinging from many lives, habit become nature; joy, anger, sorrow and pleasure flow in subtle streams. Though the truth may be suddenly penetrated, these feelings are hard to remove at once. One must constantly be aware, reducing and reducing again.” So we must be aware at every moment: as soon as a thought arises, be aware and remove it. If the delusive thought is strong and cannot be transformed for the moment, then recite the Buddha-name or hold a mantra to transform it. The Buddha-name and mantras are the sword of wisdom, used to cut off the mark-clinging deluded mind and emotional thinking; they have infinite power. If we only recite devoutly, we will certainly receive the empowerment of Buddhas and bodhisattvas; hence there is no difficulty in attaining the Way. Likewise, to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, any school will do if one makes the vow. We often say that Buddha-recitation has a very broad scope: it is not only reciting one “Amitābha” that counts as Buddha-recitation; reciting sutras is also Buddha-recitation, doing good deeds without clinging to marks is also Buddha-recitation, being alert in awakening is also Buddha-recitation. Why? Because Buddha means awakening: if you are never deluded at any moment and transfer the merit toward the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, is that not Buddha-recitation? The Pure Land school says that to attain the highest grade of the highest birth one must “read and recite the great vehicle.” Why read and recite the great vehicle? To make you understand the principle! To make you understand where birth and death and other such phenomena come from, and how to end birth and escape death. Only when you understand these principles clearly, empty the deluded mind completely, and abide nowhere, can you attain the highest grade of the highest birth. If you abide in marks and cling rigidly, thinking this world is bad and you want to go to the West to enjoy blessings, that is ruinous. Even if you can go, it will only be the lowest grade of the lowest birth. Because your mind is not empty and pure, you can only be born in the land of coexistence of sages and ordinary beings, not in the land of expedient remainder or the land of real reward and adornment.

What is Chan? It is the original, sovereign, pure mind, which the school calls “the treasury of the true Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa.” Is this wondrous mind of nirvāṇa not the Pure Land? Is it not also the secret treasury of tantra? So Chan, Pure Land and tantra appear as three schools but are in fact one body. Tantra has many methods for birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, such as the phowa method, the great Amitābha method, and the method of transferring consciousness, all for birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Reciting Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva also brings birth in the West, because Avalokiteśvara is in the West and also shines light on you and receives you to birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The reason there are nine grades of birth lies precisely in the distinction between clinging to marks and not clinging to marks! If you understand that mind is the land and the land is the mind, that birth is no-birth and no-birth is birth, and abide in no mark at all, then within no-birth there is no hindrance to being born. Such birth is wondrous function! No-birth is not dead immobility: unceasing generation is no-birth, and no-birth is unceasing generation — only thus is the wondrous truth of no-birth attained.

Therefore one should always not depart from the great natural abiding of non-cultivation.” What is called non-cultivation is “the cultivation of non-cultivation, which is true cultivation.” The Mahāmudrā is the supreme tantric method: it does not ask you to recite mantras, does not ask you to form hand-seals, does not ask you to cultivate any dharma; all is free and natural, with not the least abiding — that is it. This cultivation is the great natural abiding. After awakening in the Chan school it is the same: cultivating without cultivation, without antidotes. Antidote methods are the delusion-removing practices specially cultivated according to each person’s habits. For example, one with strong lust cultivates the contemplation of impurity and the contemplation of white bones; one who loves to talk cultivates silence, and so on — these are expedient methods for settling delusion and returning to the truth. The Mahāmudrā does not use such antidotes; it tells us that all forms are the manifestation of the self-nature, the wondrous function of the true mind, and that to be non-abiding at every moment is the great cultivation of cultivating without cultivation. For one who recites the Buddha-name, when a thought arises and as soon as one is aware it is empty, that is Buddha-recitation; it is not that one must recite one “Amitābha” to count as Buddha-recitation. But one’s practice must fit one’s own capacity and must not be forced into one mold. There are several ways of reciting the Buddha-name: to be aware as soon as a thought arises is Buddha-recitation of true mark; to contemplate oneself as Amitābha is Buddha-recitation by contemplation; to contemplate the Buddha’s marks and excellences is Buddha-recitation of marks; to be never apart from one “Amitābha” is Buddha-recitation by holding the name. In our practice we must choose a method suited to our own habits, so as to achieve twice the result with half the effort. If you cannot be empty as soon as a thought arises and you are aware, then recite the name-Buddha. If silent recitation still does not work and thoughts still stir, then recite aloud, “Amitābha...,” for you must always cut off your delusive thoughts and turn them into no-thought. It is the same Buddha-recitation, but whether one understands this principle or not makes a great difference in power. Not understanding, one clings to marks at every moment and clings to Amitābha in the West; understanding, one knows that Buddha-recitation uses Amitābha’s holy name to sweep clean the filth in our minds and to turn around the afflictions and delusions of mark-clinging, so as to realize the pure Buddha-nature that is the same as Amitābha’s. Because the methods of practice differ, the grade of one’s future birth in the West differs accordingly. This cultivation without clinging to marks is “the great natural abiding of non-cultivation”; the abiding that is no-abiding is called natural abiding.

The Chan master’s instruction says: “Where there is a Buddha, do not linger; where there is no Buddha, pass quickly by.” Where there is a Buddha, do not linger; where there is no Buddha, hurry past. This means that one may neither cling to existence nor lean toward emptiness; neither side of existence and nothingness is established, and the middle is not there either — that is the meaning of the middle way, which is the Tiantai school’s “empty, provisional, middle” threefold contemplation of the one mind. Therefore marks are not absent; they are illusorily manifested in function. If the true nature could not manifest illusory marks and function, it would be a stagnant pool — what value would Buddha-nature have? We practice in order to exhaust the deluded habit of clinging to illusory marks, not to sit there dead and motionless. If one can awaken and at every moment not abide in marks, and not cling to dharmas in practice, one is on the right road and enters “the great natural abiding of non-cultivation.”

At whatever time and in whatever place, take only the recognition of the intrinsic nature pointed out by the direct pointing as right knowing and seeing, and truly realize that this mind of ours is the one true Dharma-realm. The one true Dharma-realm encompasses all, including the myriad phenomena; any form is the wondrous function manifested by the self-mind, so do not cling to marks. Whether the circumstance is good or bad, whether it accords with my mind or goes against my wish, pay it no heed — then you see the nature at every moment. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “One who has seen the nature must see it in the words; if one is like this, then even wheeling a blade into battle, one can still see it.” Going into battle with thoughts of birth and death, of coming and going — that will not do. If I am killed, it does not matter: “I meet the white blade with my head as if cutting the spring wind,” ha ha! Cut it off and it is cut off; cut off this husk, and our true mind neither increases nor decreases, neither arises nor ceases — it still cannot be cut off. This is the conduct of one who has seen the nature.

Long ago, when Chan Master Yuangui of Mount Song was sitting in meditation, he saw an emperor standing before him with many attendants, awe-inspiring. The emperor, seeing that the Chan master did not rise to greet him, was much displeased, and asked him: “Do you know me?” The master said: “I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; how could I look on you differently?” The emperor said: “I am the mountain god, holding the power of life and death; I can make people live and make people die — how can you look at me with ordinary eyes?” The master laughed and said: “I am originally unborn; can you make an unborn person die? In my view body and space are non-dual, and you and I are non-dual; can you destroy space and yourself? Even if you could, my true mind neither arises nor ceases. What you can destroy is only my body; you cannot destroy my true mind! You have not yet realized this true mind — how can you speak of making me live or die?” The mountain god was stunned by his words: “Ah, I have never heard such words; is there still a deathless true mind?” The master continued: “For example, you are now a great god, but you were once a human being too! Only because you were upright and unswervingly just and did many good deeds have you now become a great god wielding the power of life and death. But who became the mountain god? The husk of your human life is gone; it is the consciousness-spirit that became the mountain god. That consciousness-spirit of yours is not the same as our Buddha-nature; it differs by just a little. What is the difference? With ignorance present, Buddha-nature becomes the consciousness-spirit; when ignorance is removed, the consciousness-spirit is restored to Buddha-nature. Even if ignorance remains, Buddha-nature does not decrease by a fraction, for it neither increases nor decreases. Who is it that is now the mountain god? It is this unborn, undying Buddha-nature — and you do not know it at all!” When the mountain god heard the master’s instruction, he woke as from a dream and at once took Chan Master Yuangui as his teacher and took refuge in the Buddhist order.

And those who depend on grass and cling to trees to manifest spirits — what gods are they? They are ghosts! In life they were insatiably greedy and committed offenses and fell into hell; when the punishment in hell was complete and they left it, because the habit of greed remained, they attached themselves to grass and trees, and the grass and trees became efficacious. This is truly a greedy ghost making mischief, not any god. A god is a great ghost king whose superknowledges exceed other ghosts’, but they all cling to marks. Therefore at all times, take only the recognition of the true mind indicated by the “direct pointing to the view as the school” as essential, with a mind as vast as space, so that the myriad phenomena, not one of them, are not included within our mind-nature. To restore our original capacity we must begin now: let everything go, recognize this Buddha-nature at every moment, and not abide in marks. As soon as there is abiding, recite the Buddha-name quickly, hold a mantra quickly, and best of all be empty as soon as you are aware. Understand this principle and practice — whether Pure Land, Chan or tantra — and all are easy to accomplish swiftly; without understanding this principle, all are hard to bring to fruition.
